ai-startup-funding.title: AI Startup Funding Rounds 2021–2026
ai-startup-funding.description: Deal-level funding rounds of AI companies worldwide 2021-2026, stage, amount, lead investor
ai-startup-funding.acquisition:
**How this dataset was acquired.** Every row comes from the [Radar API](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp), Fliar's company-data API and MCP server. Radar reads
business news continuously and extracts each funding announcement into structured fields: company, stage, amount, currency, investors
and date. It then links the company to its record in a database of five million companies. This release covers AI companies worldwide, January 2021 to June 2026. It runs that
output through a reproducible cleaning pipeline: repeated reports of one deal are merged, recaps of past rounds are dropped, and every
amount is checked against the sentence it was read from. Each row names the article it was read from (`news_source`, `news_url`) and
quotes the sentence (`news_excerpt`). The full, continuously updated data is available through `POST /v1/companies/funding`
([reference](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp/blob/main/docs/reference/get_company_funding.md)) or the `get_company_funding` MCP tool.
ai-startup-funding.sample_note:
**This file is a 62% sample: 5,000 of 8,122 funding rounds.** It keeps every record for a fixed subset of companies.
The subset is chosen by a hash, so it stays the same from one release to the next. The findings and tables below were computed
on the **full** data. For the rest, the withheld fields and monthly updates, [get a Radar API key](https://fliarbi.com/radar-api/developer) ([docs](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp)).
Each row's `fliar_profile_url` opens the company's full profile on Fliar.
ai-startup-funding.findings:
1. **5,412 companies raised 8,122 rounds between 2021 and mid-2026.** 6,974 rounds disclosed an amount, totalling $301.5B.
2. **2024 was the busiest year**, with 1,768 rounds. Disclosed funding in 2025 was $83.2B, 1.8× the 2021 level ($47.3B).
3. **Mega-rounds dominate the dollars.** Rounds of US$100M or more are 11% of rounds with a disclosed amount, but 67% of disclosed dollars.
4. **Early rounds got bigger.** The median Seed round went from $3.0M in 2021 to $4.8M in 2025; the median Series A from $13.0M to $16.5M.
5. **Funding is concentrated.** The top three countries (United States, United Kingdom, Canada) hold 79% of disclosed dollars.
6. **The fastest-rising sectors** (share of rounds, 2021–2022 vs 2024–2025): Business Services (3.8% → 6.0%), Enterprise Infrastructure (6.3% → 8.5%), Consumer (2.6% → 3.9%).
ai-startup-funding.method:
1. **Extraction.** Radar's pipeline reads each funding article and extracts structured fields from it, including the source sentence.
2. **Back-fill days removed.** Two days on which archived articles were loaded with the load date as their publication date (2024-04-22 and 2025-02-13) are excluded, because those rounds carry no reliable date.
3. **Scope.** Venture-style instruments only (pre-seed to Series H, growth/PE, bridge, convertible notes, venture debt, grants, strategic). IPOs, QIPs, private placements, rights issues, bank loans, bonds and acquisitions are dropped. Companies founded in 2000 or later; rounds after a company's IPO and group subsidiaries of large conglomerates are excluded.
4. **Deduplication.** Reports about the same company and stage within 45 days are one round. A round repeating an earlier amount within 180 days is dropped, as are lettered stages below one already announced (recaps). One round filed under two domains of the same company is merged.
5. **Amount check.** Each amount is compared with the money figures parsed from its source sentence (tolerance 0.6–1.7×). `verified` matched; `unchecked` had no parseable figure; `failed_check` is blank because it did not match, exceeded a stage ceiling, or was a $500M+ figure reported by one article only; `not_disclosed` had no amount.
6. **Currency.** US dollars, converted at the time of extraction and rounded to three significant figures.
7. **News columns.** The excerpt is the earliest reporting sentence that does not name a data provider. Source and URL come from that article when it can be retrieved.

8. **Sample.** Each company key is ranked by `sha1(key)`. Keys are taken in rank order until the file holds max(25%, 5,000) rows (capped at 100,000).

9. **Profile links.** Links are built from Fliar's company index and checked against it. A row whose company has no public profile has an empty link.
ai-startup-funding.limitations:
- Derived from news: rounds that were never reported are missing, and coverage is stronger for larger and English-reported deals.
- Amounts are as reported; fixed-rate conversion to US dollars makes local-currency rounds drift slightly over time.
- Stage labels mean different things in different markets.
- 2026 covers January to June only.
- Sector labels come from a company classifier, so some companies are mislabelled.
- `news_source` and `news_url` are blank when the article could not be retrieved at release time (about 40% of rows).

company-earnings-results.title: Company Earnings Results 2019–2026
company-earnings-results.description: Quarterly and annual results from business news: revenue, profit, EPS, beat/miss
company-earnings-results.acquisition:
**How this dataset was acquired.** Every row comes from the [Radar API](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp), Fliar's company-data API and MCP server. Radar reads
business news continuously and extracts each reported earnings result into structured fields: company, period, fiscal year,
currency, revenue, net income, earnings per share, growth and whether the result beat or missed expectations. It links the company to
its website in a database of five million companies. This release covers results first reported between January 2019 and June 2026.
It runs that output through a reproducible cleaning pipeline: repeated reports of the same result are merged into one row, forecasts
and previews are dropped, and each figure is checked against the sentence it was read from. Each row names the article it was read
from (`news_source`, `news_url`) and quotes the sentence (`news_excerpt`). The full, continuously updated event history, including
guidance and every reporting article, is available through `POST /v1/companies/events` ([reference](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp/blob/main/docs/reference/get_company_events.md)) or the
`get_company_events` MCP tool.
company-earnings-results.sample_note:
**This file is a 25% sample: 56,464 of 225,779 earnings results.** It keeps every record for a fixed subset of companies.
The subset is chosen by a hash, so it stays the same from one release to the next. The findings and tables below were computed
on the **full** data. For the rest, the withheld fields and monthly updates, [get a Radar API key](https://fliarbi.com/radar-api/developer) ([docs](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp)).
Each row's `fliar_profile_url` opens the company's full profile on Fliar.
company-earnings-results.findings:
1. **225,779 earnings results for 33,900 companies, reported in the news between January 2019 and June 2026.** 60,163 are full-year results, 142,897 quarterly and 22,719 half-year.
2. **35,956 results say how they compared with analyst expectations: 62% beat, 27% missed and 11% were in line.**
3. **Coverage is led by United States (79,283 results), India (45,650) and Canada (20,556)**, with 152 countries in all.
4. **Median reported full-year revenue growth** (results with US$100M+ revenue): fiscal 2019 +7.0%, fiscal 2020 +3.7%, fiscal 2021 +16.3%, fiscal 2022 +17.0%, fiscal 2023 +10.0%, fiscal 2024 +7.0%, fiscal 2025 +7.8%.
5. **28% of quarterly results with a net-income figure were losses**, from 20% (2026) to 37% (2020) by year.
6. **83% of results carry a revenue or profit figure that was found again in the reporting sentence**; 3.7% had a figure blanked because it failed the check.
company-earnings-results.method:
1. **Extraction.** Radar's pipeline reads each earnings article and extracts structured fields, including the source sentence.
2. **Scope.** Results linked to a company website and first reported between 2019-01-01 and 2026-06-30. Sentences that only preview or forecast a result (for example "is expected to report", "analysts expect") with no reported figure are dropped, as are records without any revenue, net-income or EPS figure.
3. **Periods.** Period labels are normalised to FY, H1, H2 and Q1–Q4. When the fiscal year is not stated it is read from the period text, else from the report date (a full-year, Q4 or H2 result reported in January–June belongs to the previous year).
4. **Deduplication.** All reports of the same company, fiscal year and period are one row. The row keeps the record with the widest coverage, then the most figures, then the earliest report. `report_date` is the earliest report; `news_mentions` counts the reporting articles.
5. **Amount check.** Revenue and net income are compared with every money figure in the source sentence (tolerance 0.6–1.7×). A figure is blanked when the sentence talks about that metric and gives figures with a scale word ("million", "crore") but none matches, or matches only after a power-of-ten shift (crore/lakh or million/billion slips); when it exceeds a ceiling (revenue US$700B a year, US$400B a half-year, US$200B a quarter); when net income is more than five times revenue or less than a millionth of it; or when a very large revenue (over US$20B a year, US$10B a half-year, US$5B a quarter) is not corroborated by another result of the same company within 0.4–2.5×. EPS above 100,000 and growth above 1,000% are blanked.
6. **Outlooks and market figures.** Sentences about outlook, guidance, consensus estimates, annualised run-rates, market size or combined industry revenue are dropped even when they contain a reported figure.
7. **Currency.** A "$" figure for a company in Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Singapore, Hong Kong, Chile, Mexico, Colombia, Argentina or Taiwan is read in the local currency unless the sentence says US dollars; rupee figures of Pakistani, Sri Lankan and Nepali companies use the local rupee; crore/lakh figures of Indian companies are INR; a "USD" label with no dollar in the sentence for a non-US company is cleared. US$ columns use one fixed rate per currency (approximate 2024 averages); currencies without a stable rate get no US$ figure.
8. **Normalisation.** Country names are unified (USA / US / United States → United States). Company names and sectors come from Fliar's company index where the website is known, otherwise from the article.
9. **News columns.** The excerpt is the earliest reporting sentence that names no data provider. Source and URL come from that article when it can be retrieved.

10. **Sample.** Each companie key is ranked by `sha1(key)`. Keys are taken in rank order until the file holds max(25%, 5,000) rows (capped at 100,000).

11. **Profile links.** Links are built from Fliar's company index and checked against it. A row whose company has no public profile has an empty link.
company-earnings-results.limitations:
- Derived from news: results that were never reported are missing, and coverage is stronger for large, listed and English-reported companies.
- Figures are as reported. Some articles quote adjusted or segment figures, or profit before tax where net income was expected.
- Company-to-website links are automatic; a small share of results may be attached to the wrong company website.
- US$ conversions use one fixed rate per currency, so they are for comparison, not exact.
- A few records still mix currencies inside one result (for example net income in local currency labelled US$).
- `beat_or_miss` is only present when the article said so.
- `news_source` and `news_url` are blank when the article could not be retrieved at release time (some article-store nodes were offline).
- 2026 covers January to June only.

contract-wins-2019-2026.title: Contract Wins Dataset 2019–2026: Orders & Tenders
contract-wins-2019-2026.description: Company contract wins worldwide: client, value, government, defence, IT
contract-wins-2019-2026.acquisition:
**How this dataset was acquired.** Every row comes from the [Radar API](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp), Fliar's company-data API and MCP server. Radar reads
business news and company announcements continuously, picks out sentences that report a contract win, an order or a tender award, and
extracts the contractor, the client, the value and currency, and the scope. Each party is linked to its website in a database of five
million companies, which adds country, sector and headquarters location. Repeated reports of one contract are merged into a single row,
clients that are people are excluded, clients are classed as government or private from their name, and every value is checked against
the figure in the news sentence. This release covers January 2019 to June 2026 worldwide, with dedicated tables for the United States,
the United Kingdom and India. The full, continuously updated event timeline for any company is served by `POST /v1/companies/events`
([reference](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp/blob/main/docs/reference/get_company_events.md)) and the `get_company_events` MCP tool.
contract-wins-2019-2026.sample_note:
**This file is a 25% sample: 22,576 of 90,019 contracts.** It keeps every record for a fixed subset of contractors.
The subset is chosen by a hash, so it stays the same from one release to the next. The findings and tables below were computed
on the **full** data. For the rest, the withheld fields and monthly updates, [get a Radar API key](https://fliarbi.com/radar-api/developer) ([docs](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp)).
Each row's `fliar_profile_url` opens the company's full profile on Fliar.
contract-wins-2019-2026.findings:
1. **90,019 contract wins and orders by 41,030 companies, January 2019 to June 2026.** 88% name the client organisation.
2. **Contract announcements rose from 7,244 in 2019 to 15,023 in 2025**; 2026 has 6,387 in its first half.
3. **Government is the client in 12% of contracts with a known client type.** Defence accounts for 3,126 contracts, infrastructure and construction 11,099, IT and technology 18,943.
4. **20,660 contracts (23%) disclose a value**, together $9.4T; the median is $36.0M. The largest is Boeing for Air India ($100.0B, 2023).
5. **The most frequent winner is Boeing** with 332 contracts, followed by Larsen Toubro (306) and Airbus (302).
6. **By contractor country:** United States 19,618, India 11,698, United Kingdom 6,310, Canada 4,768, Australia 3,772 contracts; 48% of contracts with a known country go to companies in the top three.
contract-wins-2019-2026.method:
1. **Extraction.** Radar's pipeline reads each news article, finds contract sentences and extracts contractor, client, value, currency, type and sector. Upstream, reports carrying the same event fingerprint are grouped and retrospective mentions are dropped.
2. **Window and dates.** The date is the publication date of the earliest report, read in Indian Standard Time; January 2019 to June 2026. Bulk archive back-fill days are dropped.
3. **Scope.** Rows typed as investments, acquisitions, sales or equity, and sentences about an acquisition with no contract wording, are dropped.
4. **Parties.** The contractor must be an organisation; rows whose client is a person are dropped, and generic or undisclosed clients ("a leading bank") are blanked. A website is kept only when the company record matches the reported name; the same company on both sides is dropped.
5. **Contract type.** From the extracted type and keywords in the sentence and client name, in priority order: Defence, Infrastructure & construction, IT & technology, Supply, Services, Maintenance & O&M, Outsourcing, Government (other), Other.
6. **Client type.** Government when the client name is a ministry, agency, public body, armed force or a known state-owned company; private for other named clients; with no client named, government only when the sentence says so.
7. **One row per contract.** Per contractor, in date order: the same client within 60 days, the same value (±3%) within 180 days, or sentences sharing half their words within 30 days are one contract. Exact repeat sentences are removed first.
8. **Countries.** Normalised (USA / US → United States). A company's country is the one most often reported for it across all its contracts (at least two reports and a majority), else the country in the report, else the company database.
9. **Amounts.** Values are converted to US$ and kept when they match a money figure in the sentence (0.6–1.7×, `verified`) or the sentence has no parseable figure and the value is plausible (`unchecked`). Values above $100B are blanked, above $10B they must be verified and reported more than once, and unchecked values above $1B are blanked.

10. **Sample.** Each contractor key is ranked by `sha1(key)`. Keys are taken in rank order until the file holds max(25%, 5,000) rows (capped at 100,000).

11. **Profile links.** Links are built from Fliar's company index and checked against it. A row whose company has no public profile has an empty link.
contract-wins-2019-2026.limitations:
- Derived from news and company announcements: unannounced contracts are missing; listed companies that must disclose orders (India in particular) are over-represented.
- ClickHouse shards were partially unavailable at build time (shard 2 down; queries skip unavailable shards), so some contracts may be missing. Article links resolve for roughly half of the rows because some article-store nodes were down.
- Contract values mix annual, multi-year and ceiling values as announced; most contracts disclose no value.
- Contract and client types are rule-based and some are wrong; state-owned companies are recognised only when well known.
- Merging is automatic: repeat orders from one client within 60 days count as one contract.
- 2026 covers January to June only.

corporate-capital-raises.title: Corporate Capital Raises 2019–2026
corporate-capital-raises.description: Equity issues, debt, private placements, rights issues, convertibles and debentures
corporate-capital-raises.acquisition:
**How this dataset was acquired.** Every row comes from the [Radar API](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp), Fliar's company-data API and MCP server. Radar reads
business news continuously and extracts each corporate capital raise into structured fields: the company, the instrument (equity issue,
debt, private placement, rights issue, convertible, debentures or preference shares), the amount, the investors or lenders and the date.
It then links the company to its record in a database of five million companies. This release covers January 2019 to June 2026 and
complements Fliar's startup funding datasets, which leave these instruments out. Repeat reports of one raise are merged, venture rounds
and capital-spending announcements are dropped, and every amount is checked against the sentence it was read from. Each row names the article
it was read from (`news_source`, `news_url`) and quotes the sentence (`news_excerpt`). A company's full, continuously updated funding history
is available through `POST /v1/companies/funding` ([reference](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp/blob/main/docs/reference/get_company_funding.md)) or the `get_company_funding` MCP tool.
corporate-capital-raises.sample_note:
**This file is a 30% sample: 5,000 of 16,402 capital raises.** It keeps every record for a fixed subset of companies.
The subset is chosen by a hash, so it stays the same from one release to the next. The findings and tables below were computed
on the **full** data. For the rest, the withheld fields and monthly updates, [get a Radar API key](https://fliarbi.com/radar-api/developer) ([docs](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp)).
Each row's `fliar_profile_url` opens the company's full profile on Fliar.
corporate-capital-raises.findings:
1. **16,402 corporate capital raises by 12,223 companies, January 2019 to June 2026.** 13,817 disclosed an amount, totalling $4.4T.
2. **Equity issues are the most common instrument** (10,451 raises), but debt carries the most disclosed money ($1.1T, median $110.0M per raise).
3. **2024 was the busiest year** with 2,876 raises; 2019 had 1,279.
4. **United States leads by count** with 2,996 raises (20% of those with a country), ahead of India (2,739) and Australia (1,510).
5. **Rights issues:** 805 in total; the most come from India (161), Nigeria (138) and Australia (105). Indian rights issues disclosed $72.4B.
6. **Billion-dollar raises:** 1,219 raises of US$1B or more are 9% of raises with an amount but 65% of disclosed dollars.
corporate-capital-raises.method:
1. **Extraction.** Radar's pipeline reads each article about a corporate capital raise and extracts structured fields, including the source sentence.
2. **Instruments.** The extracted type is normalised into seven instruments. When the sentence names a more specific instrument (rights issue, debentures or NCDs, convertible notes, preference shares, private placement, preferential allotment or QIP) that wins. Grants, IPOs and untyped rows are dropped.
3. **Scope.** Rows whose sentence does not describe raising capital are dropped, as are capital-spending announcements (a plant, a facility, an outlay) that carry no raise language, investment-fund raises (a separate dataset) and hypothetical needs ("would require raising"), and equity rows without explicit raise language (pledges to invest in a country or project). Venture rounds (seed, angel, Series A–H) are dropped because the startup funding datasets cover them.
4. **Company links.** A website whose company record matches neither the reported name nor the domain is treated as a mis-link: the reported name is kept and the domain is left blank.
5. **Deduplication.** Per company, reports of the same instrument within 45 days of a raise's first report, or of the same amount (within 5%) within 180 days, are one raise. Raises filed under name variants without a shared website (for example a name and its initials) merge when country, instrument and amount (within 1%) match within 180 days.
6. **Amount check.** Each amount is compared with the money figures parsed from its source sentence (tolerance 0.6–1.7×). `verified` matched; `unchecked` had no parseable figure; `failed_check` is blank because it did not match, was a bare number under 10,000, was over US$2B without a match, over US$5B from one article or for a company without a matched company record, or over US$25B; `not_disclosed` had no amount.
7. **Currency.** US dollars, from the stored conversion or at fixed approximate rates. In Chile, Colombia, Mexico, Argentina and Uruguay (and the Jamaican and Trinidad dollar) a bare "$" is read as the local peso unless the sentence says US dollars.
8. **Investors.** `lead_investor` is the first named investor that reads as an organisation (it has a website or an organisation word in its name); individuals are never published. Promoters and the company itself are excluded.
9. **Bulk back-fills.** Days carrying more than five times the usual number of reports (archive back-fills stamped with an ingest date rather than the publication date) are dropped.
10. **Dates.** The date is the earliest report's publication date; rows before 2019 or after June 2026 are dropped.

11. **Sample.** Each companie key is ranked by `sha1(key)`. Keys are taken in rank order until the file holds max(25%, 5,000) rows (capped at 100,000).

12. **Profile links.** Links are built from Fliar's company index and checked against it. A row whose company has no public profile has an empty link.
corporate-capital-raises.limitations:
- Derived from news: unreported raises are missing, and coverage favours large, English-reported companies and India, where exchange filings are widely reported.
- Debt covers loans, bonds and credit facilities alike; an announced facility may not be fully drawn.
- The instrument comes from a classifier and keyword rules; some raises are mis-typed.
- Some companies have no website match, so `company_domain` is blank and the name is as reported.
- Sector labels come from a company classifier, or the reported sector when the company is not matched.
- `news_source` and `news_url` are blank when the article could not be retrieved at release time.

corporate-events-2019-2026.title: Corporate Events 2019–2026: M&A, Layoffs, IPOs
corporate-events-2019-2026.description: News-reported M&A, contracts, lawsuits, layoffs, IPOs and launches per company, 2019-2026
corporate-events-2019-2026.acquisition:
**How this dataset was acquired.** Every row comes from the [Radar API](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp), Fliar's company-data API and MCP server. Radar reads
business news continuously, picks out sentences that report a corporate event (an acquisition, a contract win, a lawsuit, layoffs, an IPO,
a product launch, a regulatory decision and so on) and links each event to the company it concerns in a database of five million companies.
Where an event has two sides, Radar records which side the company was on: acquirer or target, contractor or client, plaintiff or defendant.
This release covers January 2019 to June 2026, with exact and same-day repeat reports removed. Each row carries the news sentence it was read
from and, where the article could be retrieved, its publisher and link. People-related events (leadership changes, board updates), earnings
and funding are left out; funding and capital raises are separate datasets. The full, continuously updated timeline for any company is
available through `POST /v1/companies/events` ([reference](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp/blob/main/docs/reference/get_company_events.md)) or the `get_company_events` MCP tool.
corporate-events-2019-2026.sample_note:
**This file is a 7% sample: 100,002 of 1,339,579 event reports.** It keeps every record for a fixed subset of companies.
The subset is chosen by a hash, so it stays the same from one release to the next. The findings and tables below were computed
on the **full** data. For the rest, the withheld fields and monthly updates, [get a Radar API key](https://fliarbi.com/radar-api/developer) ([docs](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp)).
Each row's `fliar_profile_url` opens the company's full profile on Fliar.
corporate-events-2019-2026.findings:
1. **1,339,579 event reports for 210,414 companies, January 2019 to June 2026.** The largest types are M&A (360,561), Company announcement (322,768), Contract (202,205), Asset acquisition (111,419).
2. **Layoff reports peaked in 2023** with 5,166 reports, against 2,122 in 2019 and 4,065 in 2025.
3. **IPO reports peaked in 2021** (8,136); 2025 had 7,978.
4. **M&A is two-sided:** 184,859 reports name the company as acquirer and 175,702 as target. The most active acquirer is KKR (651 reports), followed by Blackstone and ril.com.
5. **Coverage is concentrated:** the 50 most-reported companies hold 7.1% of all reports; Amazon alone has 10,280.
6. **Lawsuits:** 68,322 reports; the company is the defendant in 67% of those with a side.
corporate-events-2019-2026.method:
1. **Extraction.** Radar's pipeline reads each business-news article, classifies event sentences into types and links the company named to its website domain. One article can yield several events.
2. **Scope.** Thirteen event types: M&A, company announcements, contracts, asset acquisitions, lawsuits, new products, regulatory decisions, IPOs, job creation, layoffs, share buybacks, incorporations and FDA approvals. Leadership and board events (people data), earnings, and funding events are excluded.
3. **Bulk back-fills.** Days carrying more than five times the usual number of reports (archive back-fills stamped with an ingest date rather than the publication date) are dropped.
4. **Dates.** The event date is the article's publication date, read in Indian Standard Time. Rows dated before 2019 or after 30 June 2026 are dropped (the source holds some impossible dates, up to 2077).
5. **Deduplication.** The same company, event type and normalised sentence is kept once (earliest report). Reports of one company and event type on the same day whose sentences share 60% or more of their words are merged.
6. **Text.** Sentences shorter than 25 characters, sentences naming a third-party data provider and sentences carrying an email address or phone number are dropped; long sentences are cut to 300 characters.
7. **Company fields.** Name, country and sector come from Fliar's company database, joined on the domain. Countries are normalised (USA / US → United States).
8. **News columns.** Publisher and URL come from the article the sentence was read from, when it can be retrieved at release time.

9. **Sample.** Each companie key is ranked by `sha1(key)`. Keys are taken in rank order until the file holds max(25%, 5,000) rows (capped at 100,000).

10. **Profile links.** Links are built from Fliar's company index and checked against it. A row whose company has no public profile has an empty link.
corporate-events-2019-2026.limitations:
- Derived from news: unreported events are missing and coverage favours large, English-reported companies.
- A row is a deduplicated news report, not a verified transaction. A big deal reported on several days appears more than once, and a sentence can recall an older event in a newer article.
- Events are linked to the domain the company database resolves; a multinational can appear under a national domain, which also sets its country.
- Event types come from a classifier and some sentences are mis-typed.
- About 9% of domains have no match in the company database, so their name, country and sector are blank.
- 2026 covers January to June only.
- `news_source` and `news_url` are blank when the article could not be retrieved at release time.

european-company-financials.title: European Company Financials 2019–2025
european-company-financials.description: Revenue, profit, equity, assets and headcount for European companies, 2019-2025
european-company-financials.acquisition:
**How this dataset was acquired.** Every row comes from the [Radar API](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp), Fliar's company-data API and MCP server. Radar
collects the annual accounts that companies file with public company registries in the United Kingdom, France, Norway, Denmark,
Sweden, Finland and Germany, reads the structured (XBRL / iXBRL / ESEF) and published financial statements, and maps each line to a
common set of metrics. This release keeps one row per company and fiscal year (2019–2025) with five headline figures: revenue, net
income, equity, total assets and employees, in the filing currency plus a euro conversion of revenue. Every figure passed sanity
checks against the rest of the same filing. Rows are linked to the company's website where Radar can match it. The full statements
(cost lines, cash flow, debt and more, for every company) are available through `POST /v1/companies/financials`
([reference](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp/blob/main/docs/reference/get_financials.md)) or the `get_financials` MCP tool.
european-company-financials.sample_note:
**This file is a 1% sample: 100,001 of 7,275,327 company-years.** It keeps every record for a fixed subset of companies.
The subset is chosen by a hash, so it stays the same from one release to the next. The findings and tables below were computed
on the **full** data. For the rest, the withheld fields and monthly updates, [get a Radar API key](https://fliarbi.com/radar-api/developer) ([docs](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp)).
Each row's `fliar_profile_url` opens the company's full profile on Fliar.
european-company-financials.findings:
1. **7,275,327 company-years for 3,620,213 companies in seven countries, fiscal years 2019 to 2025.** The United Kingdom (2,064,089 companies) and France (933,682) are the largest groups.
2. **Revenue is filed for 42% of company-years.** Coverage runs from France 100%, Sweden 88%, Finland 85%, Norway 77%, Denmark 17%, Germany 6%, United Kingdom 3%. Most UK rows are balance sheets (equity, assets, headcount) without revenue or profit.
3. **The median company earned a net margin of 4.2%** (company-years with revenue and profit filed, n = 1,981,379); 26% of them reported a loss.
4. **Revenue is highly concentrated.** In fiscal 2024 the top 1% of companies by revenue (5,855 companies) account for 81% of the €5.0T filed revenue in the data.
5. **Among 40,193 companies with revenue of at least €1M in both 2023 and 2024, the median grew 1.7%**; 56% grew and 4% grew by half or more.
6. **Median revenue per employee** (company-years with both filed): Denmark €87.2K, Sweden €80.6K, United Kingdom €48.1K.
european-company-financials.method:
1. **Source.** Annual accounts filed with public company registries in seven countries, parsed from structured filings (XBRL, iXBRL, ESEF) and, for some German companies, from published HTML statements.
2. **One row per company-year.** Annual periods only. When a company files both single-entity and consolidated accounts for a year, the consolidated figures are used. When a year has several filings (amendments), the latest balance-sheet date wins.
3. **Metrics.** `revenue` is turnover / net sales; `net_income` is profit or loss for the year; `equity` is total shareholders' equity; `total_assets` is total assets (for UK accounts that file no total line, fixed plus current assets); `employees` is the average headcount reported in the accounts (rounded to a whole number).
4. **Sanity checks.** Values are blanked, not corrected, when: revenue or total assets are negative; a figure exceeds a ceiling (revenue €500B, net income ±€100B, equity ±€1T, total assets €5T, employees 800,000, negative headcount); equity exceeds total assets; net income is more than 10× the larger of revenue and total assets; revenue exceeds 10,000× total assets (unit errors); or a metric is filed in a different currency from the rest of the year. German HTML-parsed figures are kept only when they are exact euro-and-cent amounts, because integer values on that path were often note numbers, years or thousand-scaled. Rows with no figure left are dropped.
5. **Currency.** Money columns are in the filing currency (`currency`). `revenue_eur` and every euro figure in the tables use one fixed 2024 average rate per currency, so year-on-year growth is not affected by exchange-rate moves.
6. **Website link.** A company gets a domain when Fliar's company index links it to the company directly, or through the same national company number in the same country with a matching legal name and exactly one website.

7. **Sample.** Each companie key is ranked by `sha1(key)`. Keys are taken in rank order until the file holds max(25%, 5,000) rows (capped at 100,000).

8. **Profile links.** Links are built from Fliar's company index and checked against it. A row whose company has no public profile has an empty link.
european-company-financials.limitations:
- One storage shard of the source table was unavailable at release time, so every count is a slight undercount (one of seven storage shards, so roughly one in seven filings is missing).
- Which figures are present differs by country (see the coverage table): revenue is rare in the UK and German rows, and headcount is present only for the UK, Sweden and Denmark. German coverage is limited to filings Radar has parsed so far.
- Figures are entity-level accounts as filed. A corporate group can appear several times (holding company and subsidiaries), and consolidated and single-entity accounts are not comparable.
- Fiscal 2025 is partial because many accounts for that year had not yet been filed.
- The years covered differ by country with what Radar has collected so far: the UK and Norway are concentrated in 2023–2025, Sweden, Denmark and Germany in 2019–2021, France and Finland across the whole period. Compare countries within a year, and read trends per country.
- Most UK rows are small-company balance sheets (equity, assets, headcount) without revenue or profit.
- Euro conversions use fixed rates and are meant for ranking and banding, not for exact comparison.
- Only a small share of companies are linked to a website, so most `company_domain` and `fliar_profile_url` cells are empty.

global-startup-funding.title: Global Startup Funding Rounds 2019–2026
global-startup-funding.description: Deal-level startup funding rounds worldwide 2019-2026: stage, amount, lead investor, sector, city
global-startup-funding.acquisition:
**How this dataset was acquired.** Every row comes from the [Radar API](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp), Fliar's company-data API and MCP server. Radar reads
business news continuously and extracts each funding announcement into structured fields: company, stage, amount, currency, investors
and date. It then links the company to its record in a database of five million companies. This release covers startups worldwide, January 2019 to June 2026. It runs that
output through a reproducible cleaning pipeline: repeated reports of one deal are merged, recaps of past rounds are dropped, and every
amount is checked against the sentence it was read from. Each row names the article it was read from (`news_source`, `news_url`) and
quotes the sentence (`news_excerpt`). The full, continuously updated data is available through `POST /v1/companies/funding`
([reference](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp/blob/main/docs/reference/get_company_funding.md)) or the `get_company_funding` MCP tool.
global-startup-funding.sample_note:
**This file is a 25% sample: 20,227 of 80,911 funding rounds.** It keeps every record for a fixed subset of companies.
The subset is chosen by a hash, so it stays the same from one release to the next. The findings and tables below were computed
on the **full** data. For the rest, the withheld fields and monthly updates, [get a Radar API key](https://fliarbi.com/radar-api/developer) ([docs](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp)).
Each row's `fliar_profile_url` opens the company's full profile on Fliar.
global-startup-funding.findings:
1. **47,428 companies raised 80,911 rounds between 2019 and mid-2026.** 66,936 rounds disclosed an amount, totalling $2.3T.
2. **2021 was the busiest year**, with 14,562 rounds. Disclosed funding in 2025 was $298.4B, 1.5× the 2019 level ($200.2B).
3. **Mega-rounds dominate the dollars.** Rounds of US$100M or more are 10% of rounds with a disclosed amount, but 61% of disclosed dollars.
4. **Early rounds got bigger.** The median Seed round went from $2.1M in 2019 to $4.0M in 2025; the median Series A from $8.9M to $14.0M.
5. **Funding is concentrated.** The top three countries (United States, India, United Kingdom) hold 67% of disclosed dollars.
6. **The fastest-rising sectors** (share of rounds, 2019–2020 vs 2024–2025): Energy Tech (2.3% → 4.1%), Business Services (2.7% → 4.3%), Energy (1.4% → 2.7%).
global-startup-funding.method:
1. **Extraction.** Radar's pipeline reads each funding article and extracts structured fields from it, including the source sentence.
2. **Back-fill days removed.** Two days on which archived articles were loaded with the load date as their publication date (2024-04-22 and 2025-02-13) are excluded, because those rounds carry no reliable date.
3. **Scope.** Venture-style instruments only (pre-seed to Series H, growth/PE, bridge, convertible notes, venture debt, grants, strategic). IPOs, QIPs, private placements, rights issues, bank loans, bonds and acquisitions are dropped. Companies founded in 2000 or later; rounds after a company's IPO and group subsidiaries of large conglomerates are excluded.
4. **Deduplication.** Reports about the same company and stage within 45 days are one round. A round repeating an earlier amount within 180 days is dropped, as are lettered stages below one already announced (recaps). One round filed under two domains of the same company is merged.
5. **Amount check.** Each amount is compared with the money figures parsed from its source sentence (tolerance 0.6–1.7×). `verified` matched; `unchecked` had no parseable figure; `failed_check` is blank because it did not match, exceeded a stage ceiling, or was a $500M+ figure reported by one article only; `not_disclosed` had no amount.
6. **Currency.** US dollars, converted at the time of extraction and rounded to three significant figures.
7. **News columns.** The excerpt is the earliest reporting sentence that does not name a data provider. Source and URL come from that article when it can be retrieved.

8. **Sample.** Each company key is ranked by `sha1(key)`. Keys are taken in rank order until the file holds max(25%, 5,000) rows (capped at 100,000).

9. **Profile links.** Links are built from Fliar's company index and checked against it. A row whose company has no public profile has an empty link.
global-startup-funding.limitations:
- Derived from news: rounds that were never reported are missing, and coverage is stronger for larger and English-reported deals.
- Amounts are as reported; fixed-rate conversion to US dollars makes local-currency rounds drift slightly over time.
- Stage labels mean different things in different markets.
- 2026 covers January to June only.
- Sector labels come from a company classifier, so some companies are mislabelled.
- `news_source` and `news_url` are blank when the article could not be retrieved at release time (about 40% of rows).

google-play-apps-2026.acquisition:
**How this dataset was acquired.** Every row comes from the [Radar API](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp), Fliar's company-data API and MCP server. Radar crawls
the public Google Play store page of every app it can discover (2.94 million apps in the June 2026 crawl, read from the US storefront)
and stores each listing's title, developer, genre, install band, ratings, price, ads and in-app purchase labels and dates. This release
keeps the 1.1 million apps with at least 1,000 installs. It normalises dates to YYYY-MM-DD, reduces each developer website to its
registered domain (so apps can be joined to companies), and removes all developer contact details. The full data, including exact
install counts and install growth, is available through `POST /v1/apps/profile` ([reference](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp/blob/main/docs/reference/get_app.md)) or the `get_app` MCP tool;

google-play-apps-2026.sample_note:
**This file is a 9% sample: 100,013 of 1,101,050 apps.** It keeps every record for a fixed subset of developers.
The subset is chosen by a hash, so it stays the same from one release to the next. The findings and tables below were computed
on the **full** data. For the rest, the withheld fields and monthly updates, [get a Radar API key](https://fliarbi.com/radar-api/developer) ([docs](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp)).

google-play-apps-2026.findings:
1. **1,101,050 apps from 449,255 developers have 1,000 or more installs.** 66,992 of them (6.1%) have passed 1 million installs, and 171 have passed 1 billion.
2. **Most apps stay small.** 51% sit in the 1,000+ or 5,000+ bands; only 19.6% reach 100,000+.
3. **Games are 15% of apps but 39% of the million-install club.** Education is the largest genre (119,589 apps).
4. **Ads are the default business model.** 43% of apps show ads and 18% sell in-app purchases; only 1.4% charge to install. Among apps with 1M+ installs, 71% show ads and 51% sell in-app items.
5. **Rated apps average 4.01 stars** (median 4.2). 62% of rated apps score 4.0 or higher; 10% score below 3.0.
6. **Maintenance splits the store.** 46% of apps were updated in 2026 (up to the June crawl), while 11% have not been updated since before 2024.
google-play-apps-2026.method:
1. **Crawl.** Store pages were read between 7 and 8 June 2026 from the US storefront. Apps with fewer than 1,000 installs are left out.
2. **Install band.** `installs` is the public band label. For 98 apps the label was missing; the band was filled from the exact count, rounded down to the nearest public band.
3. **Ratings.** Score, ratings and reviews are blank when the store page showed no rating (a zero count is treated as not shown).
4. **Dates.** Release dates come in several text formats and were parsed to YYYY-MM-DD. Dates before October 2008 or after June 2026 are blank.
5. **Developer domain.** The developer website is reduced to its registered domain. Social pages, link shorteners and code hosts are blanked, as are hosts shared by ten or more unrelated developer accounts (ads.txt placeholders, site builders, free hosting). A domain is kept anyway when the package name matches it (com.facebook.* and facebook.com) or the developer name contains it.
6. **Removed.** All developer contact fields (email, address, phone, legal name and legal contacts) are dropped. Apps whose title, developer or package names a data provider, and titles carrying a phone number, are dropped. Prices above $400 are blanked.

7. **Sample.** Each developer key is ranked by `sha1(key)`. Keys are taken in rank order until the file holds max(25%, 5,000) rows (capped at 100,000).

8. **Profile links.** Links are built from Fliar's company index and checked against it. A row whose company has no public profile has an empty link.

- Read from the US storefront: apps not offered in the US often show no rating and no release date.
- Only about a third of apps show a rating; small apps usually do not have enough ratings to display one.
- Install bands are wide (for example 1,000,000+ covers 1M to 5M). Exact counts are in the API.
- A snapshot of June 2026: apps removed from the store before the crawl are not included.

india-quarterly-results.title: India Quarterly Results 2019-2026 (NSE/BSE)
india-quarterly-results.description: India quarterly results data: 32,146 company-quarters of revenue, net profit, EBITDA and YoY growth for 4,474 NSE/BSE-listed firms, Dec 2018 to Mar 2026.
india-quarterly-results.acquisition:
**How this dataset was acquired.** Every row comes from the [Radar API](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp), Fliar's company-data API and MCP server. Radar collects
the quarterly financial results that Indian listed companies file with the stock exchanges (NSE and BSE), reads the results tables and
maps each line to a common set of metrics. It also reads business news continuously and extracts the results that companies announce
(revenue, net profit, EBITDA and growth figures stated in the report), checking each figure against the sentence it came from.
This release merges the two into one row per company and quarter, from the December 2018 quarter to the March 2026 quarter, with
exchange-filed figures preferred, unit errors (lakh / crore / rupee slips) removed and year-on-year growth computed against the same
quarter a year earlier. The full quarterly income statement for any company, plus annual results, balance sheet and cash flow, is
available through `POST /v1/companies/financials` ([reference](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp/blob/main/docs/reference/get_financials.md)) or the `get_financials` MCP tool.
india-quarterly-results.sample_note:
**This file is a 25% sample: 8,039 of 32,146 company-quarters.** It keeps every record for a fixed subset of companies.
The subset is chosen by a hash, so it stays the same from one release to the next. The findings and tables below were computed
on the **full** data. For the rest, the withheld fields and monthly updates, [get a Radar API key](https://fliarbi.com/radar-api/developer) ([docs](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp)).
Each row's `fliar_profile_url` opens the company's full profile on Fliar.
india-quarterly-results.findings:
1. **32,146 quarterly results for 4,474 Indian listed companies, Q3 FY19 (Dec 2018) to Q4 FY26 (Mar 2026).** 11,518 come from stock-exchange result filings and 20,628 from results reported in business news.
2. **Latest full quarter, Q3 FY26 (Dec 2025):** 1,349 companies. Reliance Industries Ltd had the highest revenue (₹269,496 cr), followed by Bharat Petroleum (₹136,623 cr) and Hindustan Petroleum (₹124,053 cr).
3. **The median company grew revenue 11.3% year on year in Q3 FY26 (Dec 2025)**; 78% of the 627 companies with a growth figure grew.
4. **The pandemic quarter shows clearly:** median revenue growth was -7.9% in Q1 FY21 (April–June 2020), and the strongest quarter since 2021 was Q1 FY22 (Jun 2021) at +33.7% (the rebound against a depressed base).
5. **Loss-makers:** 14% of companies reporting a net profit figure in Q3 FY26 (Dec 2025) posted a loss, against 24% in Q1 FY21.
6. **Margins by sector, FY2025** (sectors with 100+ results): the highest median net margin was in Healthcare (9.6%), the lowest in Media & Entertainment (1.8%).
india-quarterly-results.method:
1. **Exchange filings.** Quarterly result statements filed with NSE and BSE (three-month periods ending March, June, September or December). When a company files both standalone and consolidated results for a quarter, the consolidated figures are used. Revenue is revenue from operations; net profit is profit after tax; EBITDA is profit before tax plus finance cost plus depreciation and amortisation (so it includes other income and exceptional items).
2. **Business news.** Results sentences extracted from business news about Indian companies, in rupees only. Forecasts, guidance and analyst estimates are dropped. A figure is kept only when the sentence carries it (`verified`) or carries no comparable figure; a figure that contradicts the sentence is dropped. The quarter is read from the period stated (for example "Q3 FY26" or "quarter ended December 2025"), else from the report date; reports more than about six months after the quarter ended are dropped.
3. **Listed companies only.** News results are kept for websites that belong to a listed company (a listed registration number, an NSE ticker or a listing record) and for banks. Bare group names ("Tata", "Reliance") that do not identify one company are dropped.
4. **Merging.** Filings and news are joined on company website and quarter. A filing figure that disagrees with a verified news figure by more than 2x is replaced by whichever is closer to the company's other quarters. The same result filed under two websites (for example a group and its namesake) is kept once.
5. **Unit errors.** Indian results are filed in rupees, thousands, lakhs, millions or crores and the unit label is sometimes wrong. A filed figure that is an exact power of ten away from the news figure or the company's other quarters is rescaled; a rupee-labelled figure under ₹10 lakh with no reference is dropped; a quarter 5x or more away from the company's median (2.5x for filed figures and large companies) is blanked; a quarter above ₹10,000 crore must be matched by another quarter of the company; a quarter above ₹1,000 crore that is more than 20x a quarter of the company's latest annual revenue is blanked.
6. **Caps.** Revenue above ₹3 lakh crore and net profit beyond ±₹40,000 crore in one quarter (above any Indian company's quarter) are blanked, as are negative revenue and EBITDA outside ±100% of revenue.
7. **Lenders and insurers.** News-reported "revenue" for banks, NBFCs and insurers mixes interest income, total income, net interest income and premiums, so for them only the exchange-filed revenue is kept, and EBITDA is left blank.
8. **Growth.** `revenue_yoy_pct` is computed against the same quarter a year earlier when both quarters come from the same kind of source and basis and neither is far from the company's usual level; otherwise the growth rate stated in the results news is used (`yoy_basis` = `reported`) when the sentence states it. Growth beyond ±1,000% is blanked.
9. **Company fields.** Names come from the filings or the news; sector from Fliar's company database; US$ at a fixed ₹1 = US$0.012.

10. **Sample.** Each company key is ranked by `sha1(key)`. Keys are taken in rank order until the file holds max(25%, 5,000) rows (capped at 100,000).

11. **Profile links.** Links are built from Fliar's company index and checked against it. A row whose company has no public profile has an empty link.
india-quarterly-results.limitations:
- Coverage is uneven over time: exchange filings were collected mostly from FY2022 on, and news coverage favours larger and more-reported companies. Counts per quarter reflect collection, not the number of listed companies; compare medians and shares.
- One storage shard of the filings table was unavailable at release time, so some filed quarters are missing.
- The March 2026 quarter (Q4 FY26) is partial: many companies had not reported, or had not been collected, by the cut-off.
- News-derived figures can be standalone or consolidated without saying so (`basis` blank), and different reports of one company can use different definitions of revenue; filed figures are more consistent.
- Figures failing a check are blanked rather than corrected, so some rows have only net profit or only revenue.
- About a quarter of filed companies are not linked to a website, so `company_domain` and `fliar_profile_url` are empty for them.
- Companies whose fiscal year does not end in March are labelled with the Indian fiscal calendar by quarter-end month.
- Sector labels come from a company database and are broad.

india-salary-benchmarks-2026.title: India Salary Data 2026: 49k Job Postings
india-salary-benchmarks-2026.description: India salary data 2026: 49,355 job postings with posted pay in INR per year by role, seniority, city and industry, Indian job market Jan 2024 to Jun 2026.
india-salary-benchmarks-2026.acquisition:
**How this dataset was acquired.** Every row comes from the [Radar API](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp), Fliar's company-data API and MCP server. Radar reads
public job postings from job boards and company career pages every day and parses each one into structured fields: title, employer,
location, experience asked, category and pay. This release keeps the Indian postings that state a salary, published between January 2024
and June 2026, removes re-posts of the same job, and converts every pay figure (annual, monthly, or "lakh per annum") to **rupees per
year**. It is built for salary benchmarking: percentiles by role family, seniority, city, industry and experience band. It holds no job
descriptions, application links or recruiter names. Salary statistics for any title, city and skill set, refreshed daily, are served by
`POST /v1/jobs/salary-benchmark` ([reference](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp/blob/main/docs/reference/salary_benchmark.md)) or the `salary_benchmark` MCP tool; the postings themselves by `POST /v1/jobs/search`.
india-salary-benchmarks-2026.sample_note:
**This file is a 26% sample: 12,958 of 49,355 salaried job postings.** It keeps every record for a fixed subset of companies.
The subset is chosen by a hash, so it stays the same from one release to the next. The findings and tables below were computed
on the **full** data. For the rest, the withheld fields and monthly updates, [get a Radar API key](https://fliarbi.com/radar-api/developer) ([docs](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp)).
Each row's `fliar_profile_url` opens the company's full profile on Fliar.
india-salary-benchmarks-2026.findings:
1. **49,355 Indian job postings with a stated salary from 10,015 employers**, posted January 2024 to June 2026 (21,575 of them in 2026). The median posted salary is **₹6.5L a year** (middle half: ₹3.5L to ₹12.0L).
2. **Product & project management pays most among role families** (median ₹11.0L), followed by devops & cloud (₹10.2L); customer service pays least (₹3.1L), a 3.6× gap.
3. **Experience multiplies pay**: the median rises from ₹3.0L for 0–1 years asked to ₹8.5L at 4–6 years and ₹17.5L at 11–15 years, about 6× the entry level.
4. **The highest medians among cities with 500+ salaried postings**: Bengaluru (₹7.5L), Gurugram (₹7.2L) and Pune (₹7.2L); the lowest is Kolkata (₹4.5L). Bengaluru alone carries 24% of salaried postings.
5. **Software engineering is the biggest salaried role family** (12,094 postings, 25%); its median is ₹7.8L, and senior software postings ask a median ₹10.0L.
6. **Internships and trainee roles** (2,134 postings) offer a median ₹1.5L a year (≈ ₹12,500 a month); 13% of all postings are linked to a company website.
india-salary-benchmarks-2026.method:
1. **Scope.** Postings located in India with a title, an employer and a stated salary, published 2024-01-01 to 2026-06-30.
2. **Deduplication.** Postings with the same employer, normalised title and month are one posting; the copy with the most structured fields is kept.
3. **Pay normalisation (INR per year).** Monthly pay × 12. Figures between 1 and 60 in an annual field are lakhs per annum (× 100,000). Figures between ₹1,000 and ₹99,999 in an annual field are monthly pay (mostly internship stipends) and are multiplied by 12. A lower bound below a tenth of the upper bound (for example "0 – 10,00,000") is treated as missing, and the midpoint is then the single posted figure.
4. **Absurd values dropped.** Postings are dropped when the annual figure falls below ₹30,000 or above ₹2.5 crore, when an internship pays more than ₹15 lakh, when an annual figure lies between 60 and 999 (neither lakhs nor rupees), when an internship figure would only make sense as lakhs, when pay is hourly or daily in rupees, or when the currency is not INR (248 postings in all: intern pay above ceiling 80, above ceiling 63, below floor 46, currency differs from country 33, ambiguous rupee figure 24, hourly/daily rupee pay 2).
5. **Overseas and spam postings removed.** 482 postings for jobs abroad (a foreign country as the location or in the title, typically overseas placement offers) and 210 postings from 6 employers that advertise low-wage jobs at senior pay (for example customer service at ₹40 lakh) or scatter dozens of unrelated roles over several states at ₹15 lakh+ are dropped as job-scam patterns.
6. **Labels.** `role_family` comes from the posting when it has one, else from keyword rules on the title, else from the category. `seniority` comes from the title (intern, junior, senior, lead, manager, director, VP/C-level); when the title has no signal it is derived from the years asked (≤1 entry, 2–5 mid, 6–10 senior, 11+ lead). `industry_category` maps the free-text and coded categories into 20 groups.
7. **Privacy and provenance.** URLs, source names, descriptions and recruiter details are not published; posting IDs are hashes. Postings whose employer or title names a job board or data provider are dropped, and phone- or e-mail-like strings are removed from titles.
8. **Company link.** `company_domain` is filled only when the lower-cased employer name matches exactly one Indian company in Fliar's company index.

9. **Sample.** Each company key is ranked by `sha1(key)`. Keys are taken in rank order until the file holds max(25%, 5,000) rows (capped at 100,000).

10. **Profile links.** Links are built from Fliar's company index and checked against it. A row whose company has no public profile has an empty link.
india-salary-benchmarks-2026.limitations:
- Only a minority of Indian postings state a salary; employers that publish pay (startups, staffing firms, mid-market companies) are over-represented and large IT services firms are under-represented.
- Posted pay is an offer range, not realised pay, and often excludes variable pay and benefits.
- Collection is uneven over time: April–May 2025 and May–June 2026 dominate, so month-to-month changes mix collection with hiring.
- Unit errors remain possible where a monthly figure looked plausible as an annual one; obvious cases were converted or dropped.
- Role families and seniority are keyword-based and can be wrong for unusual titles.
- Most employers are not linked to a website because their names match no single company in the index.

india-startup-funding.title: Indian Startup Funding Rounds 2015–2026
india-startup-funding.description: Deal-level Indian startup rounds 2015-2026 with stage, amount, lead investor and profile links
india-startup-funding.acquisition:
**How this dataset was acquired.** Every row comes from the [Radar API](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp), Fliar's company-data API and MCP server. Radar reads
business news continuously and extracts each funding announcement into structured fields: company, stage, amount, currency, investors
and date. It then links the company to its record in a database of five million companies. This release covers startups based in India, January 2015 to June 2026. It runs that
output through a reproducible cleaning pipeline: repeated reports of one deal are merged, recaps of past rounds are dropped, and every
amount is checked against the sentence it was read from. Each row names the article it was read from (`news_source`, `news_url`) and
quotes the sentence (`news_excerpt`). The full, continuously updated data is available through `POST /v1/companies/funding`
([reference](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp/blob/main/docs/reference/get_company_funding.md)) or the `get_company_funding` MCP tool.
india-startup-funding.sample_note:
**This file is a 37% sample: 5,006 of 13,697 funding rounds.** It keeps every record for a fixed subset of companies.
The subset is chosen by a hash, so it stays the same from one release to the next. The findings and tables below were computed
on the **full** data. For the rest, the withheld fields and monthly updates, [get a Radar API key](https://fliarbi.com/radar-api/developer) ([docs](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp)).
Each row's `fliar_profile_url` opens the company's full profile on Fliar.
india-startup-funding.findings:
1. **6,128 companies raised 13,697 rounds between 2015 and mid-2026.** 10,927 rounds disclosed an amount, totalling $258.0B.
2. **2021 was the busiest year**, with 1,853 rounds. Disclosed funding in 2025 was $21.4B, 1.5× the 2015 level ($14.4B).
3. **Mega-rounds dominate the dollars.** Rounds of US$100M or more are 7% of rounds with a disclosed amount, but 59% of disclosed dollars.
4. **Early rounds got bigger.** The median Seed round went from $500.0K in 2015 to $1.3M in 2025; the median Series A from $5.0M to $6.0M.
5. **Funding is concentrated.** The top three cities (Bengaluru, Mumbai, Gurugram) hold 69% of disclosed dollars.
6. **The fastest-rising sectors** (share of rounds, 2015–2016 vs 2024–2025): Energy Tech (0.7% → 5.2%), High Tech (1.3% → 5.4%), Fintech (8.6% → 11.4%).
india-startup-funding.method:
1. **Extraction.** Radar's pipeline reads each funding article and extracts structured fields from it, including the source sentence.
2. **Back-fill days removed.** Two days on which archived articles were loaded with the load date as their publication date (2024-04-22 and 2025-02-13) are excluded, because those rounds carry no reliable date.
3. **Scope.** Venture-style instruments only (pre-seed to Series H, growth/PE, bridge, convertible notes, venture debt, grants, strategic). IPOs, QIPs, private placements, rights issues, bank loans, bonds and acquisitions are dropped. Companies founded in 2000 or later; rounds after a company's IPO and group subsidiaries of large conglomerates are excluded.
4. **Deduplication.** Reports about the same company and stage within 45 days are one round. A round repeating an earlier amount within 180 days is dropped, as are lettered stages below one already announced (recaps). One round filed under two domains of the same company is merged.
5. **Amount check.** Each amount is compared with the money figures parsed from its source sentence (tolerance 0.6–1.7×). `verified` matched; `unchecked` had no parseable figure; `failed_check` is blank because it did not match, exceeded a stage ceiling, or was a $500M+ figure reported by one article only; `not_disclosed` had no amount.
6. **Currency.** US dollars, converted at the time of extraction and rounded to three significant figures.
7. **News columns.** The excerpt is the earliest reporting sentence that does not name a data provider. Source and URL come from that article when it can be retrieved.

8. **Sample.** Each company key is ranked by `sha1(key)`. Keys are taken in rank order until the file holds max(25%, 5,000) rows (capped at 100,000).

9. **Profile links.** Links are built from Fliar's company index and checked against it. A row whose company has no public profile has an empty link.
india-startup-funding.limitations:
- Derived from news: rounds that were never reported are missing, and coverage is stronger for larger and English-reported deals.
- Amounts are as reported; fixed-rate conversion to US dollars makes local-currency rounds drift slightly over time.
- Stage labels mean different things in different markets.
- 2026 covers January to June only.
- Sector labels come from a company classifier, so some companies are mislabelled.
- `news_source` and `news_url` are blank when the article could not be retrieved at release time (about 40% of rows).

investor-coinvestment-network.title: VC Co-Investment Network: 303k Investor Pairs
investor-coinvestment-network.description: VC co-investment network: 303,421 pairs of startup investors (VC, CVC, PE) that backed the same funding round worldwide, 2019 to mid-2026.
investor-coinvestment-network.acquisition:
**How this dataset was acquired.** Every row is derived from the [Radar API](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp), Fliar's company-data API and MCP server.
Radar reads business news continuously and extracts each startup funding announcement into structured fields, including every
named investor. Those rounds are cleaned (repeated reports merged, recaps dropped), people and generic phrases are removed from the
investor lists, and every pair of investor organisations that appeared in the same round becomes one edge here, weighted by the
number of rounds they shared between January 2019 and June 2026. Each investor's profile and portfolio are available through
`POST /v1/investors/page` ([reference](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp/blob/main/docs/reference/get_investor_page.md)) or the `get_investor_page` MCP tool.
investor-coinvestment-network.sample_note:
**This file is a 25% sample: 75,855 of 303,421 investor pairs.** It keeps every record for a fixed subset of pairs.
The subset is chosen by a hash, so it stays the same from one release to the next. The findings and tables below were computed
on the **full** data. For the rest, the withheld fields and monthly updates, [get a Radar API key](https://fliarbi.com/radar-api/developer) ([docs](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp)).
Each row's `fliar_profile_url` opens the company's full profile on Fliar.
investor-coinvestment-network.findings:
1. **303,421 investor pairs co-invested at least once** across 42,182 rounds with two or more named organisation investors (65% of rounds with any), January 2019 to June 2026. 50,836 pairs (17%) did so two or more times and 829 ten or more times.
2. **The strongest pair is Sequoia Capital and Tiger Global**, with 87 shared rounds; next are Soma Capital and Y Combinator (84) and Lightspeed Venture Partners and Sequoia Capital (72).
3. **Y Combinator has the widest network**: it shared a round with 1,738 different investors. Tiger Global (1,480) and Gaingels (1,404) follow.
4. **Syndicates grew in the 2021 boom.** The average number of named organisation investors per round was 2.72 in 2019, 3.21 in 2021, 2.93 in 2023, 3.13 in 2025.
5. **Like backs like.** 64% of pairs join two investors of the same type; VC–VC pairs are 60% of all pairs, VC–CVC 8% and VC–PE 9%.
investor-coinvestment-network.method:
1. **Rounds and investors.** The same cleaned rounds and the same organisation-only investor list as the VC investor directory release: January 2019 to June 2026, people, generic phrases ("angel investors", "existing investors") and data providers removed, aliases merged (a16z = Andreessen Horowitz). Two archive back-fill days (2024-04-22 and 2025-02-13) are excluded.
2. **Same family.** Pairs of a firm and its own regional arm or fund vehicle (Sequoia Capital + Sequoia Capital India, Softbank + SoftBank Vision Fund 2, Goldman Sachs + Goldman Sachs Alternatives) are removed: news often names both for one cheque.
3. **Edges.** Every unordered pair of distinct investor organisations named in the same round is an edge; `shared_deals` counts the rounds. The pair is written in alphabetical order of the names, so each pair appears once.
4. **Sector and country.** `top_shared_sector` and `top_shared_country` are the most frequent sector and company country across the shared rounds.
5. **Types.** The investor types come from the directory release (rule-based: VC, CVC, PE, accelerator, bank-debt, government, other).
6. **Sample.** Pairs are sampled whole by a hash of the pair; an investor's edges are therefore spread across the sample, not kept together. Degree and other network measures in the report are computed on the full edge list.

7. **Sample.** Each pair key is ranked by `sha1(key)`. Keys are taken in rank order until the file holds max(25%, 5,000) rows (capped at 100,000).

8. **Profile links.** Links are built from Fliar's company index and checked against it. A row whose company has no public profile has an empty link.
investor-coinvestment-network.limitations:
- Built from news: rounds that were never reported are missing, and reports often name only some of the investors, so weak ties are under-counted.
- An edge means the two investors were named in the same round, not that they negotiated together.
- Investor names come from article text; a few aliases stay split, which splits their edges too.
- Because the sample is a random 25% of edges, network measures computed on the sample (degree, centrality) are lower than on the full graph.
- 2026 covers January to June only.

ipo-tracker-2019-2026.title: IPO Data 2019-2026: India, US, UK & Global IPOs
ipo-tracker-2019-2026.description: IPO dataset: 13,316 company IPOs from January 2019 to June 2026 across India (NSE, BSE, SME), the US, UK and 100+ countries, with issue size and exchange.
ipo-tracker-2019-2026.acquisition:
**How this dataset was acquired.** Every row comes from the [Radar API](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp), Fliar's company-data API and MCP server. Radar reads
business news continuously, picks out sentences about initial public offerings (filings, price bands, subscriptions, pricing, listings,
withdrawals) and extracts the company, exchange, issue size, price band, issue price and dates, linking each company to its website in
a database of five million companies. This release collapses about 129,000 such reports into one row per company IPO, from January 2019 to
June 2026: India's mainboard (NSE, BSE) and SME platforms (NSE Emerge, BSE SME) in depth, plus the United States, the United Kingdom and
more than 100 other countries. Each row says whether a report confirmed the listing, carries the issue size only when it matches a money
figure in the report's own sentence, and quotes that sentence with its publisher where the article could be retrieved. The full event
timeline for any company, including follow-on offerings and every source article, is available through `POST /v1/companies/events`
([reference](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp/blob/main/docs/reference/get_company_events.md)) or the `get_company_events` MCP tool.
ipo-tracker-2019-2026.sample_note:
**This file is a 38% sample: 5,000 of 13,316 company IPOs.** It keeps every record for a fixed subset of companies.
The subset is chosen by a hash, so it stays the same from one release to the next. The findings and tables below were computed
on the **full** data. For the rest, the withheld fields and monthly updates, [get a Radar API key](https://fliarbi.com/radar-api/developer) ([docs](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp)).
Each row's `fliar_profile_url` opens the company's full profile on Fliar.
ipo-tracker-2019-2026.findings:
1. **13,316 company IPOs, January 2019 to June 2026, one row per company.** 3,014 have a report that the shares listed or the issue was priced; 186 were reported withdrawn or postponed; the rest were announced or filed.
2. **The United States (3,412 IPOs, 26%) and India (2,913, 22%) lead**, far ahead of China (841), Canada (723) and the United Kingdom (486). Of the Indian IPOs with a known board, 941 are SME issues and 955 mainboard.
3. **Indian SME IPOs took off after 2022:** 85 in 2022, 164 in 2023, 276 in 2024 and 268 in 2025. The median SME issue with a verified size is ₹31 cr; the median mainboard issue is ₹650 cr.
4. **2021 was the peak year** (2,857 IPOs, 323 of them blank-check SPACs), against 920 in 2019, 1,615 in 2022 and 2,225 in 2025. Completed listings were 697 in 2021 and 557 in 2025.
5. **Largest completed IPO: SpaceX** ($75.0B, Nasdaq, 2026), then Saudi Aramco ($29.4B, 2019) and Rivian ($12.0B). India's largest is Hyundai Motor Company (₹27,390 cr, 2024).
6. **SPACs:** 690 blank-check IPOs and 785 companies that went public by merging with one; 47% of the blank-check IPOs are dated 2021.
ipo-tracker-2019-2026.method:
1. **Extraction.** Radar's pipeline reads each business-news article, classifies IPO sentences and extracts the company, exchange, currency, issue size, price band, issue price, listing date and IPO type. Follow-on offerings, offers for sale on their own, QIPs and rights issues are excluded.
2. **One row per company IPO.** Reports are grouped by the company's website; reports with only a name join the website their name maps to. Name variants are then merged in four passes: one name's words start the other's or the names are 90%+ similar (same year, compatible country); a short and long name on the same exchange and year (Uber / Uber Technologies); the same verified US$200M+ amount in the same year under related names (ADNOC / ADNOC Gas); a name-only report whose words contain a linked company's full name. Series numbers keep SPACs apart (Acquisition II vs III). A handful of merges were made by hand after reading the largest rows.
3. **Names.** Descriptions are stripped ("Saudi Arabia's state-owned oil giant Aramco" → Aramco); placeholders, exchanges, people and descriptions ("Zomato-backed startup") are dropped.
4. **Status.** `Completed` needs a report sentence that names the company and says the shares listed, debuted or began trading, the issue was priced or oversubscribed, or the IPO raised money, with no plan language (will, expected, plans, filed, draft) unless the sentence also says the stock debuted or traded. `Withdrawn / postponed` is a company with a quarter or more of its reports about a suspension, withdrawal, postponement or cancellation and no trading report.
5. **Dates and year.** The listing date is taken from completion reports and must fall within 120 days before to 30 days after the article. The IPO year is the listing year, else the year most completion reports were written, else the year of the first report. IPOs listed before 2019 (recalled in later articles) are dropped, as are companies known only from roundup articles that name six or more IPOs. Reports from archive back-fill days (dates carrying five times the usual volume, old articles stamped with an ingest date; 7,023 reports) are dropped.
6. **Issue size.** A figure stands when (a) its currency is written in the sentence, (b) it matches a money figure in the sentence (0.6–1.7×), (c) it does not sit next to a valuation, deal-value, revenue or subscription-demand word, and (d) the sentence reports a completed IPO or concrete offer terms (price band, fresh issue, offer for sale, lot size) without target or valuation language. For a completed IPO the completion reports are used. The figure most distinct sentences agree on wins. Amounts above US$80B are dropped (the largest in the data is US$75B). Indian SME amounts above US$60M are dropped. SPAC-merger "sizes" (deal values) are blanked.
7. **Hand checks.** The largest rows were read against their sentences: a rights issue, a follow-on offering and preferred-stock deals were removed, and amounts that were another figure were blanked (listed in the spec).
8. **Exchange and board.** About 2,600 exchange spellings are mapped to 80 exchanges. Indian issues are Mainboard (NSE, BSE) or SME (NSE Emerge, BSE SME, or an SME issue whose exchange is not stated).
9. **Company fields.** Country is the reports' company country, else the company database, else the exchange's country. Sector is read from the reports, else from the company database, and grouped into 20 broad sectors.
10. **News columns.** The excerpt is the earliest clean report sentence, preferring one whose article can be retrieved at release time.

11. **Sample.** Each company key is ranked by `sha1(key)`. Keys are taken in rank order until the file holds max(25%, 5,000) rows (capped at 100,000).

12. **Profile links.** Links are built from Fliar's company index and checked against it. A row whose company has no public profile has an empty link.
ipo-tracker-2019-2026.limitations:
- Derived from news: IPOs that were never reported are missing, and coverage favours English-language reporting. Year-to-year counts also reflect how much news was ingested; the 2025 jump in announced IPOs is partly wider news coverage.
- Most rows are announcements or filings without a completion report (`Announced / filed`); many of those did list, others never happened. Use `listing_status == "Completed"` for listings.
- Issue sizes are as reported in the news (some include the greenshoe, some do not) and only about one row in five has one; the US$ figure uses the reported dollar amount or a fixed average exchange rate.
- Company matching is automatic: some companies still appear twice under name variants, and a few rows are linked to the wrong website (a parent or a namesake).
- The full ₹ issue size is shown for Indian rows; US$-only figures are converted at ₹83 = US$1 in the India tables.
- 2026 covers January to June only.
- `news_source` and `news_url` are blank when the article could not be retrieved at release time (some article stores were offline).
