job-postings-2026.title: Job Postings 2026: India and United States
job-postings-2026.description: Deduplicated job postings Jan-Jun 2026 with role, skills, salary and location
job-postings-2026.acquisition:
**How this dataset was acquired.** Every row comes from the [Radar API](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp), Fliar's company-data API and MCP server. Radar
collects public job postings across job boards and company career pages every day, parses each one into structured fields (title,
employer, location, work mode, experience, education, skills and pay) and normalises salaries to an annual US-dollar figure. This
release covers postings published in India and the United States between January and June 2026, deduplicated so that a job
re-posted on several sites appears once. It contains no description text, no application links and no recruiter names. The full,
daily-updated postings, with filters for skills, salary, experience and freshness, are available through `POST /v1/jobs/search`
([reference](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp/blob/main/docs/reference/search_jobs.md)) or the `search_jobs` MCP tool.
job-postings-2026.sample_note:
**This file is a 6% sample: 100,009 of 1,654,294 job postings.** It keeps every record for a fixed subset of companies.
The subset is chosen by a hash, so it stays the same from one release to the next. The findings and tables below were computed
on the **full** data. For the rest, the withheld fields and monthly updates, [get a Radar API key](https://fliarbi.com/radar-api/developer) ([docs](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp)).
Each row's `fliar_profile_url` opens the company's full profile on Fliar.
job-postings-2026.findings:
1. **1,654,294 distinct job postings from 240,895 employers, January to June 2026**: 1,320,685 in the United States and 333,609 in India.
2. **14% of postings state a salary.** Median annualised pay: US $60.0K, India $8.7K; 91% of salaried postings are in the US.
3. **Few postings advertise remote work.** Postings marked remote (in the work-mode field or the title): 1.1% in India, 1.6% in United States; hybrid: 0.2% in India, 0.4% in United States.
4. **The most requested skills** across 458,559 postings that list skills: python (40,630), sql (30,259), excel (28,234), aws (18,795), java (18,370).
5. **Healthcare is the largest role family (20% of postings with a role)**, followed by sales (10%) and finance (7%).
6. **Tech pay gap:** the median salaried software, data or cloud posting offers $116.5K in the US and $18.3K in India, 6× apart at market exchange rates.
job-postings-2026.method:
1. **Scope.** Postings with a title and employer, located in India or the United States, published 2026-01-01 to 2026-06-30.
2. **Deduplication.** Postings with the same employer, normalised title and month are one posting; the copy with the most structured fields (role, salary, skills, category) is kept.
3. **Privacy and provenance.** URLs, source names, descriptions and recruiter details are not published. Posting IDs are a hash, not the source ID. Phone-number-like and e-mail-like strings are removed from titles; postings whose employer or title names a job board or data provider are dropped.
4. **Labels.** `role` and `seniority` come from the posting when it has them; otherwise they are inferred from the title with keyword rules (blank when no rule fits). `category` unifies occupation codes (mapped to their major occupation group) and free-text categories. `remote` is read from the posting and from "remote" / "hybrid" in the title.
5. **Salary.** Annualised from the posted range and pay unit (hourly × 2,080, weekly × 52, monthly × 12) and converted to US$. Kept only when a currency was given and the value lies between US$10,000 and US$1,000,000 (US) or US$1,200 and US$500,000 (India); otherwise blank.
6. **Experience.** Minimum years asked, 1–40; zero or not stated is blank.
7. **Company link.** A posting gets a `company_domain` only when its lower-cased employer name matches exactly one company in Fliar's company index in the same country.

8. **Sample.** Each companie key is ranked by `sha1(key)`. Keys are taken in rank order until the file holds max(25%, 5,000) rows (capped at 100,000).

9. **Profile links.** Links are built from Fliar's company index and checked against it. A row whose company has no public profile has an empty link.
job-postings-2026.limitations:
- Collection is uneven over time: India counts grow sharply from January to June 2026, so month-to-month counts reflect collection as well as hiring.
- Some posted salaries carry the wrong pay unit (for example weekly pay annualised as monthly); obvious cases are blanked, others remain.
- A posting is not a hire; some postings are evergreen or advertise several openings.
- Inferred roles and seniority are keyword-based and can be wrong for unusual titles.
- Salary is posted for a minority of jobs, mostly in the United States, so salary statistics describe salaried postings only.
- Employer names are as posted (including staffing agencies), and most are not linked to a website.
- Deduplication is by employer, title and month: the same job posted in two months appears twice.

lawsuits-2019-2026.acquisition:
**How this dataset was acquired.** Every row comes from the [Radar API](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp), Fliar's company-data API and MCP server. Radar reads

person are left out entirely, so every row is between organisations (or a company and unnamed investors, consumers or employees).
Repeated reports of one case are merged into a single row and every amount is checked against the figure in the news sentence. This
release covers January 2019 to June 2026 worldwide, with dedicated tables for the United States, the United Kingdom and India. The full,
continuously updated event timeline for any company is served by `POST /v1/companies/events` ([reference](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp/blob/main/docs/reference/get_company_events.md)) and the
`get_company_events` MCP tool.
lawsuits-2019-2026.sample_note:
**This file is a 25% sample: 5,517 of 22,071 cases.** It keeps every record for a fixed subset of companies.
The subset is chosen by a hash, so it stays the same from one release to the next. The findings and tables below were computed
on the **full** data. For the rest, the withheld fields and monthly updates, [get a Radar API key](https://fliarbi.com/radar-api/developer) ([docs](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp)).
Each row's `fliar_profile_url` opens the company's full profile on Fliar.
lawsuits-2019-2026.findings:
1. **22,071 corporate lawsuits and enforcement cases involving 13,412 companies, January 2019 to June 2026.** The company is the defendant in 89% of cases.
2. **Case reports rose from 2,151 in 2019 to a peak of 4,260 in 2024.** The largest types are civil (10,570), regulatory (5,593), class action (2,937), criminal (1,003).
3. **A government body or regulator is the opponent in 2,862 cases (13%).**
4. **By jurisdiction:** United States 10,321, India 2,900, United Kingdom 941, Canada 616, Germany 594 cases; the United States alone accounts for 50% of cases with a known jurisdiction.
5. **The most-sued company is Google** (76 cases as defendant), followed by Amazon (60) and Apple (56).
6. **2,494 cases report a settlement, fine or award**, together $1.3T; the largest is BHP ($31.7B, 2024).
lawsuits-2019-2026.method:
1. **Extraction.** Radar's pipeline reads each news article, finds sentences about legal cases and extracts plaintiffs, defendants, case type, court, status and amounts. Upstream, reports carrying the same event fingerprint are grouped and retrospective mentions dropped.
2. **Window and dates.** The date is the publication date of the earliest report, read in Indian Standard Time; January 2019 to June 2026. Bulk archive back-fill days are dropped.
3. **No people.** A case is dropped when any plaintiff or defendant is a named person (recognised by name shape against a list of given names, or by a job title such as CEO or founder). Law firms announcing class actions are not treated as parties.
4. **Company and opponent.** The row's company is the first organisational defendant, else the plaintiff; the opponent is the first organisation on the other side. Opponents are typed as government / regulator from their name, else company; unnamed investors, consumers or employees are "shareholders / class". A website is kept only when the company record matches the reported name.
5. **One row per case.** Per company, in date order within a year: the same opponent, the same case type within 90 days, or sentences sharing half their words within 60 days are one case. The latest reported status is kept.
6. **Amounts.** Claims and settlements are converted to US$ and kept when they match a money figure in the sentence or are plausible with no figure to check; among reports, the value most others agree with wins. Values above $200B are blanked, above $20B they must be verified and reported more than once, and unchecked values above $1B are blanked.

7. **Sample.** Each company key is ranked by `sha1(key)`. Keys are taken in rank order until the file holds max(25%, 5,000) rows (capped at 100,000).

8. **Profile links.** Links are built from Fliar's company index and checked against it. A row whose company has no public profile has an empty link.
lawsuits-2019-2026.limitations:
- Derived from news: unreported cases are missing; US securities class actions are heavily covered because law firms publish press releases about them.
- ClickHouse shards were partially unavailable at build time (shard 2 down; queries skip unavailable shards), so some cases may be missing. Article links resolve for roughly half of the rows because some article-store nodes were down.
- Excluding every case with a named person removes many disputes that also involve executives.
- Case type, status and party roles come from a classifier and some are wrong; one long case can be split into several rows when reports are more than a year apart.
- 2026 covers January to June only.

layoffs-2019-2026.title: Layoffs Dataset 2019–2026: Global, India, US, UK
layoffs-2019-2026.description: Company layoffs worldwide: jobs cut, % of workforce, country, sector
layoffs-2019-2026.acquisition:
**How this dataset was acquired.** Every row comes from the [Radar API](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp), Fliar's company-data API and MCP server. Radar reads
business news continuously in many countries and languages, picks out sentences that report job cuts, and extracts the company, the
number of jobs cut, the share of the workforce and the country. Each company is linked to its website in a database of five million
companies, which adds its home country, headquarters state or city and sector. Repeated reports of one layoff round are merged into a
single row (same company within 45 days), sector-wide or unnamed employers are dropped, and every headcount and percentage is kept only
when it appears in the news sentence. The data covers January 2019 to June 2026 worldwide, with India, the United Kingdom and the rest of
the world outside the US given dedicated tables. The full, continuously updated event timeline for any company is served by
`POST /v1/companies/events` ([reference](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp/blob/main/docs/reference/get_company_events.md)) and the `get_company_events` MCP tool.
layoffs-2019-2026.sample_note:
**This file is a 26% sample: 5,000 of 19,208 layoff events.** It keeps every record for a fixed subset of companies.
The subset is chosen by a hash, so it stays the same from one release to the next. The findings and tables below were computed
on the **full** data. For the rest, the withheld fields and monthly updates, [get a Radar API key](https://fliarbi.com/radar-api/developer) ([docs](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp)).
Each row's `fliar_profile_url` opens the company's full profile on Fliar.
layoffs-2019-2026.findings:
1. **19,208 layoff events at 13,303 companies in 169 countries, January 2019 to June 2026.** 57% of events with a known country happened outside the United States.
2. **Layoff events peaked in 2020** (3,780 events); 2023 had 3,391 and 2025 had 2,977, against 1,759 in 2019.
3. **India: 971 layoff events**, peaking in 2023 (219); the United Kingdom has 2,198. 9,541 events state a verified headcount, together 10,929,045 jobs; the median cut is 195.
4. **The largest single permanent cut is Amazon** (99,000 jobs, July 2022, United States); 540 events are furloughs or temporary lay-offs, flagged in `is_furlough`.
5. **2,768 companies had more than one layoff round**; 371 had five or more.
6. **Retail has the most layoff events** (1,008), followed by Food and Agriculture (795) and Consumer Goods (773).
layoffs-2019-2026.method:
1. **Extraction.** Radar's pipeline reads each news article, finds sentences reporting job cuts and extracts company, headcount, share of workforce and country. Upstream, reports carrying the same event fingerprint are grouped and retrospective mentions are dropped.
2. **Window and dates.** The date is the publication date of the earliest report, read in Indian Standard Time; January 2019 to June 2026. Bulk archive back-fill days (over five times the usual volume) are dropped.
3. **Companies.** Descriptor prefixes are removed ("Tata Motors-owned Jaguar Land Rover" → Jaguar Land Rover). Rows naming a person, an unnamed or generic employer ("the company") or a whole sector ("IT companies") are dropped. A website is kept only when the company record matches the reported name.
4. **One row per layoff round.** Reports of the same company within 45 days of the round's first report (and not in a different stated country) are one event. Exact repeat sentences are removed first.
5. **Headcount and %.** A headcount is kept only when the same number (±2%, including "1.2 lakh", "10k", "a dozen") appears in the sentence; the earliest verified figure of the round is used. Headcounts above 150,000 are blanked. The share of workforce is kept only when the sentence states it (a percentage, "half", "a third").
6. **Countries.** `country` is the country where the cut happens as reported, else the company's home country; names are normalised (USA / US → United States).

7. **Sample.** Each company key is ranked by `sha1(key)`. Keys are taken in rank order until the file holds max(25%, 5,000) rows (capped at 100,000).

8. **Profile links.** Links are built from Fliar's company index and checked against it. A row whose company has no public profile has an empty link.
layoffs-2019-2026.limitations:
- Derived from news: unreported layoffs are missing, and coverage favours large companies and English-language media; India and Europe are well covered, many emerging markets thinly.
- ClickHouse shards were partially unavailable at build time (shard 2 down; queries skip unavailable shards), so some layoffs may be missing. Article links resolve for roughly half of the rows because some article-store nodes were down.
- Many reports give no headcount, or a figure that could not be verified; jobs-cut totals sum only verified headcounts and understate the true total.
- Merging is automatic: two separate rounds at one company within 45 days count as one, and a long-running restructuring may be split.
- Sector and HQ location are known only for companies matched to the company database.
- News ingest thins after May 2026; 2026 covers January to June only.

mergers-acquisitions-2019-2026.description: Mergers and acquisitions worldwide: acquirer, target, deal value, US, UK, India
mergers-acquisitions-2019-2026.acquisition:
**How this dataset was acquired.** Every row comes from the [Radar API](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp), Fliar's company-data API and MCP server. Radar reads
business news continuously, picks out sentences that report an acquisition, a merger or a stake purchase, and extracts the acquirer, the
target, the deal value and currency, the share acquired and the deal status. Each party is linked to its website in a database of five
million companies, which adds its country, sector and headquarters location. Repeated reports of one deal (announcement, approval,
completion, follow-up coverage) are merged into a single row, rumours and "in talks" reports are left out, parties that are people or
undisclosed buyers are dropped, and every deal value is checked against the figure in the news sentence. This release covers January
2019 to June 2026 worldwide, with dedicated tables for the United States, the United Kingdom and India. The full, continuously updated
deal history for any company is served by `POST /v1/companies/events` ([reference](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp/blob/main/docs/reference/get_company_events.md)) and the `get_company_events` MCP tool.
mergers-acquisitions-2019-2026.sample_note:
**This file is a 25% sample: 30,887 of 123,550 deals.** It keeps every record for a fixed subset of acquirers.
The subset is chosen by a hash, so it stays the same from one release to the next. The findings and tables below were computed
on the **full** data. For the rest, the withheld fields and monthly updates, [get a Radar API key](https://fliarbi.com/radar-api/developer) ([docs](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp)).
Each row's `fliar_profile_url` opens the company's full profile on Fliar.
mergers-acquisitions-2019-2026.findings:
1. **123,550 M&A deals between 65,109 acquirers and 107,767 targets, January 2019 to June 2026.** 84% are acquisitions of control, 6% mergers and 9% minority stakes.
2. **Deal count peaked in 2025** with 20,854 deals, against 10,424 in 2019. 2026 has 10,818 in its first half.
3. **29,882 deals (24%) disclose a value**, together $24.2T; the median disclosed deal is $100.0M. The largest is United Technologies / Raytheon ($120.0B, 2019).
4. **43% of deals with both countries known are cross-border.** US companies are on one side of 54,058 deals, UK companies 17,114 and Indian companies 8,970; 1,725 deals bring a foreign acquirer into India.
5. **The most active acquirer is Accenture** with 231 deals, followed by KKR (186) and Blackstone (128).
6. **37,896 deals are reported completed and 718 terminated**; the rest were last reported as announced or pending.
mergers-acquisitions-2019-2026.method:
1. **Extraction.** Radar's pipeline reads each business-news article, finds M&A sentences and extracts acquirer, target, value, currency, stake, status and date. Upstream, reports carrying the same event fingerprint are grouped and retrospective mentions of old deals are dropped.
2. **Window and dates.** The announced date is the publication date of the earliest report, read in Indian Standard Time; January 2019 to June 2026. Days carrying a bulk archive back-fill (over five times the usual volume) are dropped.
3. **Parties.** Descriptor prefixes are removed ("Chrysler parent Stellantis" → Stellantis). Deals are dropped when either party is a person, an undisclosed or generic party ("an unnamed buyer", "the company") or the same company on both sides. A website linked to a party is kept only when the company record matches the reported name; otherwise the name is kept and the website blanked.
4. **Rumours.** Reports flagged as rumoured, or worded as talks, considerations or potential bids, are dropped.
5. **Deal type.** Merger when reported as one; stake when the share acquired is under 50% (or a stake purchase without control wording); acquisition otherwise.
6. **One row per deal.** Reports naming the same target and the same (or an alias of the) acquirer within 365 days are one deal; a second pass merges target name variants (with and without a website) under one acquirer. The latest reported status wins, and completion overrides announcement.
7. **Amounts.** Values are converted to US$ (stored US$ value, or the native amount at 2023–2025 average rates) and kept only when they match a money figure in the sentence (0.6–1.7×) — `verified` — or when the sentence has no parseable figure and the value is plausible — `unchecked`. Values above $300B are blanked, above $25B they must be verified and reported more than once, and unchecked values above $2B are blanked. "$" in Latin-American deals is read as the local peso unless US dollars are named.
8. **Countries and sectors.** Countries are normalised (USA / US → United States). A company's country is the one most often reported for it across all its deals (at least two reports and a majority), else the country in the report, else the company database. Sector is the target's Fliar sector label.

9. **Sample.** Each acquirer key is ranked by `sha1(key)`. Keys are taken in rank order until the file holds max(25%, 5,000) rows (capped at 100,000).

10. **Profile links.** Links are built from Fliar's company index and checked against it. A row whose company has no public profile has an empty link.
mergers-acquisitions-2019-2026.limitations:
- Derived from news: unreported deals are missing and coverage favours large, English-reported companies.
- ClickHouse shards were partially unavailable at build time (shard 2 down; queries skip unavailable shards), so some deals may be missing. Article links resolve for roughly half of the deals because some article-store nodes were down.
- Deal values are as reported at announcement and mix equity and enterprise values; about two-thirds of deals disclose no value.
- Merging is automatic: a few deals may remain split across name variants, and a repeat purchase from the same seller within a year is merged into one deal.
- Country, state and city come from the extraction or the company database; a multinational may appear under a national website.
- Deal types and statuses come from a classifier and some are wrong.
- 2026 covers January to June only.

open-company-database.acquisition:
**How this dataset was acquired.** Every row comes from the [Radar API](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp), Fliar's company-data API and MCP server. Radar builds
its company database by merging public company registries, company websites, business news and job postings into one record per company,
keyed by the company's website domain. Each record is classified into a sector, industry and business model by Radar's own models and
carries headquarters location, founding year, funding status and size. This release keeps the firmographic core of the five million
companies that have both a name and a website: one row per domain, with country names normalised and founding years checked. The full
records, with financials, funding, people and technology, are available through `POST /v1/companies/profile`
([reference](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp/blob/main/docs/reference/get_company.md)) or the `get_company` MCP tool.
open-company-database.sample_note:
**This file is a 2% sample: 100,000 of 4,863,273 companies.** It keeps every record for a fixed subset of domains.
The subset is chosen by a hash, so it stays the same from one release to the next. The findings and tables below were computed
on the **full** data. For the rest, the withheld fields and monthly updates, [get a Radar API key](https://fliarbi.com/radar-api/developer) ([docs](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp)).
Each row's `fliar_profile_url` opens the company's full profile on Fliar.
open-company-database.findings:
1. **4,863,273 companies with a working website.** 3,233,643 (66%) have a known country, spread over 228 countries; 65% have a founding year.
2. **The United States holds 34% of companies with a known country**, followed by India (10.6%), United Kingdom (10.1%), Canada (4.6%), Germany (3.6%).
3. **A young population.** The median founding year is 2013; 45% of dated companies were founded in 2015 or later and 80% in 2000 or later.
4. **9.0% have raised outside funding.** 35% are recorded as unfunded, 7.4% as acquired, 1.7% as public and 8.4% as closed.
5. **Business Services is the largest sector** (16% of classified companies), ahead of Consumer and Real Estate and Construction.
6. **Funding is concentrated in tech sectors.** Life Sciences (38%), High Tech (23%), Fintech (20%) have the highest funded shares among the 30 largest sectors, against 9% overall.
open-company-database.method:
1. **Scope.** Every company in Radar's database with a name and a website, as of October 2026.
2. **One row per domain.** Domains are lowercased with the scheme, `www.` and any path removed. When several records share a domain, the most complete one (founding year, sector, country, city, status, size) is kept.
3. **Country.** Country names are normalised (for example "england, united kingdom", "uk" and "dubai united arab emirates" become "United Kingdom" / "United Arab Emirates"). Values that are not a country, such as state names or codes, are blank.
4. **Founding year.** Years before 1800 or after 2026 are blank.
5. **Labels.** Sector is the first practice area and industry the first listed industry; business model keeps up to three tags. Status "Closed" is a company recorded as shut down.
6. **Removed.** Companies whose name or domain names a data provider, and names containing a phone number, are dropped. No revenue, funding amounts, investors, people, contacts, descriptions or technology fields are published.

7. **Sample.** Each domain key is ranked by `sha1(key)`. Keys are taken in rank order until the file holds max(25%, 5,000) rows (capped at 100,000).

8. **Profile links.** Links are built from Fliar's company index and checked against it. A row whose company has no public profile has an empty link.
open-company-database.limitations:
- The database leans toward companies with an online presence and toward English-speaking markets; it is not a census of all firms.
- Country is unknown for about a third of companies, and city for a larger share; they are blank, not guessed.
- Status and funding flags are only as current as the last update of each record; "Unfunded" means no funding is recorded.
- Recent founding years are under-counted, because new companies enter the database with a lag.
- Employee bands are available for about one company in five.
- This file is a 2% sample (capped at 100,000 rows); the tables above use all five million companies.

skill-salary-percentiles-global.title: Global Salary Data by Skill & Role (620k jobs)
skill-salary-percentiles-global.description: Global salary data by skill and role: 620,752 job postings in 55 countries with pay in US$ per year, US vs UK vs India vs rest of world, Jan 2024 to Jun 2026.
skill-salary-percentiles-global.acquisition:
**How this dataset was acquired.** Every row comes from the [Radar API](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp), Fliar's company-data API and MCP server. Radar reads
public job postings from job boards and company career pages in many countries every day and parses each one into structured fields:
title, employer, location, category, skills and pay. This release keeps the postings that state pay, published between January 2024 and
June 2026, removes re-posts, annualises every figure and converts it to **US dollars per year with one stated exchange-rate table**, so
skills, roles and countries can be compared on one scale. It holds no job descriptions, application links or recruiter names. Salary
statistics for any title, city, currency and skill set, refreshed daily, are served by `POST /v1/jobs/salary-benchmark`
([reference](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp/blob/main/docs/reference/salary_benchmark.md)) or the `salary_benchmark` MCP tool.
skill-salary-percentiles-global.sample_note:
**This file is a 16% sample: 100,060 of 620,752 job postings with pay.** It keeps every record for a fixed subset of companies.
The subset is chosen by a hash, so it stays the same from one release to the next. The findings and tables below were computed
on the **full** data. For the rest, the withheld fields and monthly updates, [get a Radar API key](https://fliarbi.com/radar-api/developer) ([docs](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp)).
Each row's `fliar_profile_url` opens the company's full profile on Fliar.
skill-salary-percentiles-global.findings:
1. **620,752 job postings with stated pay from 137,004 employers in 55 countries**, January 2024 to June 2026, every figure annualised and converted to US$. 56% are in the United States; 22 countries have at least 30 postings and 14 have at least 400.
2. **Country medians span 24×** among the 14 countries with 400+ postings: Switzerland $117,470, United States $60,000, Ireland $55,319, Austria $53,933 at the top; India $7,558, Brazil $4,896 at the bottom.
3. **Software engineering pays a median $120,805 in the US**, $78,947 in the UK and $9,012 in India at market exchange rates, a 13× US–India gap.
4. **109,469 postings carry skill tags.** Among skills with 200+ US postings the best paid are ai ($134,000), c++ ($131,000), aws ($128,000), kubernetes ($125,750).
5. **In India the best-paid tagged skills** (200+ postings) are ca ($31,977), llm ($31,977), microservices architecture ($31,395), bfsi sales ($29,070), against a national median of $7,558.
6. **The UK sample is small** (2,129 postings, median $46,581): few UK postings in the collection state pay, so UK figures carry wide uncertainty. 1,553 postings with absurd or unconvertible pay were dropped before any statistic was computed.
skill-salary-percentiles-global.method:
1. **Scope.** Postings with a title, an employer, a country and stated pay, published 2024-01-01 to 2026-06-30.
2. **Deduplication.** Postings with the same employer, normalised title and month are one posting; the copy with the most structured fields is kept.
3. **Annualisation.** Hourly × 2,080, daily × 260, weekly × 52, bi-weekly × 26, semi-monthly × 24, monthly × 12. Indian figures between 1 and 60 in an annual field are lakhs per annum; Indian figures between ₹1,000 and ₹99,999 in an annual field are monthly pay. Singapore listings from one board that carried monthly pay multiplied by 144 are divided by 12. Postings without a currency take the country's own currency.
4. **Currency conversion.** One fixed table of approximate 2025 average market rates (units per US$): AED 3.6725, AUD 1.55, BRL 5.6, CAD 1.4, CHF 0.83, CLP 950, COP 4100, CZK 22.5, EUR 0.89, GBP 0.76, HKD 7.8, HUF 360, IDR 16400, ILS 3.6, INR 86, JPY 150, MXN 19.3, MYR 4.35, NZD 1.72, PEN 3.7, PHP 57.5, PLN 3.8, QAR 3.64, RON 4.45, SAR 3.75, SEK 10, SGD 1.31, THB 33.5, TRY 39, UAH 41, USD 1, UYU 40, VND 25500, ZAR 18. The full table, with posting counts, is printed above.
5. **Absurd values dropped, and how many.** Annual pay below US$15,000 (US), US$10,000 (other high-income countries), ₹30,000 (India) or US$1,200 (elsewhere); above US$1,000,000 (US), ₹2.5 crore (India) or US$600,000 (elsewhere); weekly travel-contract healthcare pay annualised with the wrong unit; implausible hourly, weekly or low-wage-title figures; postings whose currency differs from the country's own (for example US jobs posted in rupees); Indian overseas-placement and job-scam postings. Counts: currency differs from country 538, below floor 372, weekly travel-contract pay mislabelled 309, implausible for role 80, intern pay above ceiling 80, above ceiling 73, implausible hourly rate 55, ambiguous rupee figure 24, currency not convertible 19, hourly/daily rupee pay 2, implausible weekly rate 1; Indian overseas postings 482; Indian job-scam postings 210.
6. **Labels.** `role_family` from the posting, else keyword rules on the (mostly English) title, else the category. `seniority` from the posting or title, else from years asked. `region_group` puts every country other than the US, UK and India in "Rest of world".
7. **Privacy and provenance.** URLs, source names, descriptions and recruiter details are not published; posting IDs are hashes. Postings whose employer or title names a job board or data provider are dropped.

8. **Sample.** Each company key is ranked by `sha1(key)`. Keys are taken in rank order until the file holds max(25%, 5,000) rows (capped at 100,000).

9. **Profile links.** Links are built from Fliar's company index and checked against it. A row whose company has no public profile has an empty link.
skill-salary-percentiles-global.limitations:
- Coverage is very uneven by country: the United States, Canada, France, India and Germany hold most postings; 33 countries have fewer than 30 postings and the UK only about 2,100. Country figures under a few hundred postings are indicative.
- The queue idea expected 47 countries with skill-level detail. Skill tags exist mainly on US, Indian and Singapore postings, so skill percentiles describe those markets; elsewhere the dataset supports role-level percentiles only.
- Fixed exchange rates convert currencies but do not adjust for purchasing power or for exchange-rate moves over 2024–2026.
- Posted pay is an offer, not realised pay; it usually excludes bonus, equity and benefits. Hourly pay is annualised at 2,080 hours.
- Role keyword rules are English; non-English titles (France, Germany) fall more often into "other".
- Collection is uneven over time, with most rows in 2026; month-to-month changes mix collection with hiring.

uk-company-financials-2019-2025.acquisition:
**How this dataset was acquired.** Every row comes from the [Radar API](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp), Fliar's company-data API and MCP server. Radar

legal form, the incorporation year, the size class of its accounts and the region of its registered office (from the postcode area

turnover, profit after tax, total assets, equity and employees. Every figure passed sanity checks against the rest of the same
filing, and companies named after a private individual are left out. Rows are linked to the company's website where Radar can match
it. The full accounts (cash, debtors, creditors, borrowings, cost lines and more, for every company) are available through
`POST /v1/companies/financials` ([reference](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp/blob/main/docs/reference/get_financials.md)) or the `get_financials` MCP tool.

**This file is a 3% sample: 100,000 of 3,861,907 company-years.** It keeps every record for a fixed subset of companies.
The subset is chosen by a hash, so it stays the same from one release to the next. The findings and tables below were computed
on the **full** data. For the rest, the withheld fields and monthly updates, [get a Radar API key](https://fliarbi.com/radar-api/developer) ([docs](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp)).

uk-company-financials-2019-2025.findings:
1. **3,861,907 company-years for 1,988,626 UK companies, fiscal years 2019 to 2025.** Coverage is densest in recent years: 578,252 companies in 2023, 1,759,265 in 2024 and 1,508,193 in 2025.
2. **Most UK accounts are balance sheets.** Total assets are present on 73% of company-years, equity on 99% and headcount on 79%, but turnover on only 2.6% and profit on 4.0%: small and micro companies may file without a profit and loss account.
3. **18% of UK companies reported negative equity in fiscal 2024** (liabilities above assets), out of 1,734,786 companies that filed equity. The median company held £56.3K of total assets and £2.8K of equity.
4. **London is home to 26% of companies with a known region in fiscal 2024 but 71% of their combined total assets**: the large banks and insurers that lead the total-assets table are registered there.
5. **The median company that filed a profit and loss account earned a 3.7% net margin** (n = 86,183 company-years); 32% reported a loss.
6. **Among 3,799 companies with turnover of at least £1M in both 2023 and 2024, the median grew 2.8%**; 57% grew and 43% shrank.

uk-company-financials-2019-2025.method:
1. **Source.** Annual accounts filed with the UK public company register (public company registry filings), parsed from structured iXBRL accounts, joined on the company number to the register snapshot of May 2026 for SIC code, legal form, status, incorporation date, accounts size class and registered-office postcode.
2. **One row per company-year.** Annual periods only. When a company files both single-entity and consolidated accounts for a year, the consolidated figures are used; when a year has several filings (amendments), the latest balance-sheet date wins. Two source records with the same company number and year are merged into the one with more figures.
3. **Metrics.** `turnover` is turnover / revenue; `profit` is profit or loss for the financial year after tax; `equity` is shareholders' funds; `total_assets` is total assets, or fixed plus current assets for the many small-company accounts that file no total line; `employees` is the average headcount (rounded).
4. **Sanity checks.** Values are blanked, not corrected, when: turnover or total assets are negative; a figure exceeds a ceiling (turnover £400B, profit ±£80B, equity ±£800B, total assets £4T); equity exceeds total assets; profit is more than 10x the larger of turnover and total assets; turnover exceeds 1,000x total assets above £10M (unit errors); a headcount above 1,000 that the company's turnover or assets cannot support, or above 800,000; or a metric is filed in a different currency from the rest of the year. Rows with no figure left are dropped.
5. **Region.** The registered office's postcode area is mapped to the twelve UK regions and nations; the register's own country field decides Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland when present. Companies registered in the Crown Dependencies and overseas entities are dropped. Postcodes and addresses are not published.
6. **Sector.** The first SIC 2007 code on the register, mapped to its section and two-digit division. 99999 (dormant) and 74990 (non-trading) are kept as their own labels.
7. **Personal names.** Companies whose name is only a person's first name and surname (for example "Jane Smith Ltd") are one-person businesses named after their owner and are dropped, as are names starting with Mr/Mrs/Ms/Dr. The test uses a list of common first names, so it removes most but not all such names.
8. **Currency.** Money columns are in the filing currency (GBP for almost every row). Tables convert other currencies at fixed 2024 rates.
9. **Website link.** A company gets a domain when Fliar's company index links it directly, or through the same company number with a matching name and exactly one website.

10. **Sample.** Each company key is ranked by `sha1(key)`. Keys are taken in rank order until the file holds max(25%, 5,000) rows (capped at 100,000).

11. **Profile links.** Links are built from Fliar's company index and checked against it. A row whose company has no public profile has an empty link.

- Register attributes (status, accounts type, SIC, region) come from the May 2026 snapshot, not from the year of the accounts; companies that have since left the register have blank attributes.

uk-startup-funding-2019-2026.acquisition:
**How this dataset was acquired.** Every row comes from the [Radar API](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp), Fliar's company-data API and MCP server. Radar reads
business news continuously and extracts each funding announcement into structured fields: company, stage, amount, currency, investors
and date. It then links the company to its record in a database of five million companies. This release covers startups based in the United Kingdom, January 2019 to June 2026. It runs that
output through a reproducible cleaning pipeline: repeated reports of one deal are merged, recaps of past rounds are dropped, and every
amount is checked against the sentence it was read from. Each row names the article it was read from (`news_source`, `news_url`) and
quotes the sentence (`news_excerpt`). The full, continuously updated data is available through `POST /v1/companies/funding`
([reference](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp/blob/main/docs/reference/get_company_funding.md)) or the `get_company_funding` MCP tool.

uk-startup-funding-2019-2026.findings:
1. **4,099 companies raised 6,676 rounds between 2019 and mid-2026.** 5,551 rounds disclosed an amount, totalling $161.0B.
2. **2021 was the busiest year**, with 1,189 rounds. Disclosed funding in 2025 was $16.3B, 1.1× the 2019 level ($15.5B).
3. **Mega-rounds dominate the dollars.** Rounds of US$100M or more are 8% of rounds with a disclosed amount, but 62% of disclosed dollars.
4. **Early rounds got bigger.** The median Seed round went from $2.0M in 2019 to $4.1M in 2025; the median Series A from $7.5M to $12.0M.
5. **Funding is concentrated.** The top three cities (London, Cambridge, Bristol) hold 70% of disclosed dollars.
6. **The fastest-rising sectors** (share of rounds, 2019–2020 vs 2024–2025): Energy Tech (3.4% → 5.4%), Business Services (4.2% → 6.1%), Healthtech (4.7% → 6.5%).
7. **By nation, England holds 96.4% of disclosed dollars** ($151.0B); Scotland $3.8B (2.4%, 451 rounds), Wales $1.2B (0.7%, 122 rounds), Northern Ireland $773.6M (0.5%, 85 rounds).
uk-startup-funding-2019-2026.method:
1. **Extraction.** Radar's pipeline reads each funding article and extracts structured fields from it, including the source sentence.
2. **Scope.** Venture-style instruments only (pre-seed to Series H, growth/PE, bridge, convertible notes, venture debt, grants, strategic). IPOs, QIPs, private placements, rights issues, bank loans, bonds and acquisitions are dropped. Companies founded in 2000 or later; rounds after a company's IPO and group subsidiaries of large conglomerates are excluded.
3. **Deduplication.** Reports about the same company and stage within 45 days are one round. A round repeating an earlier amount within 180 days is dropped, as are lettered stages below one already announced (recaps). One round filed under two domains of the same company is merged.
4. **Amount check.** Each amount is compared with the money figures parsed from its source sentence (tolerance 0.6–1.7×). `verified` matched; `unchecked` had no parseable figure; `failed_check` is blank because it did not match, exceeded a stage ceiling, or was a $500M+ figure reported by one article only; `not_disclosed` had no amount.
5. **Currency.** US dollars, converted at the time of extraction and rounded to three significant figures.
6. **News columns.** The excerpt is the earliest reporting sentence that does not name a data provider. Source and URL come from that article when it can be retrieved.
7. **Not a completed round.** Rounds whose every report describes talks or plans ("in talks to raise", "seeking", "plans to commit") are dropped, and undisclosed-stage, debt or strategic rounds that read as project or asset finance (solar and wind projects, MW capacity, tax equity, financing packages) are dropped.
8. **Location check.** Companies whose rounds mostly name cities that are almost never in the United Kingdom across the global table (under 5% of 10 or more rounds) are dropped: their website was matched to a same-named foreign company, or the company only has a holding entity here.
9. **Back-fill days.** Two days on which archives of older articles were loaded with the load date instead of the publication date (2024-04-22 and 2025-02-13) are excluded.
10. **Nation.** From the company's record in the company register; when it has none, the most common nation of companies in the same city in this data.

11. **Sample.** Each company key is ranked by `sha1(key)`. Keys are taken in rank order until the file holds max(25%, 5,000) rows (capped at 100,000).

12. **Profile links.** Links are built from Fliar's company index and checked against it. A row whose company has no public profile has an empty link.

us-quarterly-results.description: US quarterly earnings data: 136,343 company-quarters of revenue, net income and operating income for 7,615 US listed companies, Q1 2019 to Q2 2026.

**How this dataset was acquired.** Every row comes from the [Radar API](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp), Fliar's company-data API and MCP server. Radar
collects the structured (XBRL) quarterly reports (form 10-Q) and annual reports (form 10-K) that US listed companies file with the US
securities regulator, maps each reported line to a common set of metrics, and keeps one row per company and fiscal quarter. This
release covers quarters ending January 2019 to June 2026 with three headline lines (revenue, net income and operating income, in US$)
and year-on-year growth computed against the same fiscal quarter a year earlier. Q4 is not filed on its own, so it is derived as the
annual figure minus the nine-month year-to-date when both cover the same fiscal year. Each company carries its ticker, SIC sector and,
where Radar can match it, its website. The full statements (cost lines, EPS, cash flow, balance sheet) for every quarter are available
through `POST /v1/companies/financials` ([reference](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp/blob/main/docs/reference/get_financials.md)) or the `get_financials` MCP tool.

**This file is a 25% sample: 34,093 of 136,343 company-quarters.** It keeps every record for a fixed subset of companies.
The subset is chosen by a hash, so it stays the same from one release to the next. The findings and tables below were computed
on the **full** data. For the rest, the withheld fields and monthly updates, [get a Radar API key](https://fliarbi.com/radar-api/developer) ([docs](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp)).

us-quarterly-results.findings:
1. **136,343 company-quarters for 7,615 US-listed companies, quarters ending January 2019 to June 2026.** 95,101 rows carry revenue, 129,387 net income and 108,494 operating income.
2. **Latest full quarter (2025Q4):** 4,192 companies reported a combined $4.7T of revenue and $495.9B of net income. AMAZON COM INC had the largest revenue ($213.4B), Apple Inc. the largest profit ($42.1B).
3. **Most filers lose money:** only 52.8% of companies with a net-income line were profitable in 2025Q4, against 79.5% of the 624 companies with at least $1B of quarterly revenue.
4. **Concentration:** the 50 largest companies by revenue took 48.7% of all revenue reported for 2025Q4, and the 50 most profitable earned 56.9% of all profits.
5. **Growth:** the median company grew revenue 5.5% year on year in 2025Q4 (companies with at least $1M of revenue a year earlier); the median was 26.0% in the 2021Q2 rebound and -9.8% in 2020Q2.
6. **Coverage over time:** 5,376 companies at the peak (2022Q1) and 4,192 in 2025Q4; 31,683 Q4 rows are derived from the annual report minus nine months.
us-quarterly-results.method:
1. **Source.** Structured XBRL data from 10-Q and 10-K filings (and their amendments) filed with the US securities regulator, consolidated figures in US dollars only. Filers reporting in another currency are left out.
2. **Quarters.** Q1–Q3 are the three-month figures reported in each 10-Q (not the year-to-date). Q4 = the 10-K annual figure minus the nine-month year-to-date of the Q3 10-Q, used only when both start on the same date and the year ends 80–100 days after the nine months (`q4_derived` = True).
3. **One row per company-quarter.** When a quarter was filed more than once (amendments, restated comparatives), the latest filing wins. A quarter that appears under two fiscal-year labels is kept once (by period end).
4. **Sanity checks.** Values are blanked, not corrected, when: revenue is negative; a quarterly figure exceeds a ceiling (revenue $250B, net or operating income ±$100B); a figure is more than 300× above or below the same company's median quarter (scale slips, for companies with at least four quarters and a median above $1M); quarterly revenue exceeds six times total assets (unit errors); operating income exceeds twice revenue for a company with $100M+ revenue; or a derived Q4 revenue is below a quarter or above four times the average of the same year's Q1–Q3 (the annual report was restated, for example for discontinued operations). Rows with no figure left are dropped, and periods ending after 30 June 2026 are excluded.
5. **Revenue fallback.** For filers that tag no revenue line, revenue = gross profit + cost of revenue when both are filed for the quarter.
6. **Not operating companies.** Exchange-traded funds, commodity, bitcoin and royalty trusts, and investment funds are dropped by name and SIC code (6189, 6221, 6722, 6726).
7. **Calendar quarter.** Bucketed from the period end minus 15 days, so a 52/53-week quarter ending on 4 October counts as Q3; each company has at most one row per calendar quarter.
8. **Growth.** `revenue_yoy_pct` compares with the same fiscal quarter of the prior fiscal year when the two period ends are 350–380 days apart and prior revenue is positive. Rankings and medians use only companies with at least $1M of revenue a year earlier.
9. **Sector.** From the latest SIC code the company filed, grouped into readable sectors (with pharmaceuticals, biotech, software, semiconductors, REITs and blank-check companies split out).
10. **Website and venue.** A company gets a domain when Fliar's company index links its filings to a website directly, or through a unique US ticker whose company name matches. The listing venue comes from the same ticker match.

11. **Sample.** Each company key is ranked by `sha1(key)`. Keys are taken in rank order until the file holds max(25%, 5,000) rows (capped at 100,000).

12. **Profile links.** Links are built from Fliar's company index and checked against it. A row whose company has no public profile has an empty link.
us-quarterly-results.limitations:
- One storage shard of the source table was unavailable at release time, so some company-quarters are missing (a slight, roughly even undercount).
- Revenue is not tagged by every filer (banks and insurers often report other income lines), so revenue is blank for a share of rows; net income is the most complete line.
- Q4 is derived, so it absorbs any year-end adjustments and restatements of earlier quarters.
- Quarters ending in 2026 are partial: many companies had not filed their 2026 reports at release time.
- Fiscal years differ by company; use `calendar_quarter` to compare companies at the same point in time.
- The file includes small and shell companies quoted over the counter alongside large caps; filter by revenue for like-for-like analysis.
- Totals across companies are sums over whoever filed in that quarter, not a fixed index.
- Only part of the companies are linked to a website, so some `company_domain` and `fliar_profile_url` cells are empty.

us-salary-benchmarks-2026.title: US Salary Data 2026: 350k Job Postings
us-salary-benchmarks-2026.description: US salary data 2026: 350,000 job postings with posted pay in US$ per year by role, seniority, state, metro area and industry, Jan 2024 to Jun 2026.
us-salary-benchmarks-2026.acquisition:
**How this dataset was acquired.** Every row comes from the [Radar API](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp), Fliar's company-data API and MCP server. Radar reads
public job postings from job boards and company career pages every day and parses each one into structured fields: title, employer,
location, work mode, experience asked, category and pay. This release keeps the United States postings that state pay, published between
January 2024 and June 2026, removes re-posts of the same job, and annualises every pay figure (hourly, weekly, monthly or annual) to
**US dollars per year**. It is built for salary benchmarking by role family, seniority, state, metro area, industry and experience. It holds
no job descriptions, application links or recruiter names. Salary statistics for any title, city and skill set, refreshed daily, are served
by `POST /v1/jobs/salary-benchmark` ([reference](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp/blob/main/docs/reference/salary_benchmark.md)) or the `salary_benchmark` MCP tool; the postings themselves by `POST /v1/jobs/search`.
us-salary-benchmarks-2026.sample_note:
**This file is a 25% sample: 88,798 of 350,328 job postings with pay.** It keeps every record for a fixed subset of companies.
The subset is chosen by a hash, so it stays the same from one release to the next. The findings and tables below were computed
on the **full** data. For the rest, the withheld fields and monthly updates, [get a Radar API key](https://fliarbi.com/radar-api/developer) ([docs](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp)).
Each row's `fliar_profile_url` opens the company's full profile on Fliar.
us-salary-benchmarks-2026.findings:
1. **350,328 US job postings that state pay, from 73,471 employers**, posted January 2024 to June 2026 (222,579 in 2026). The median posted pay is **$60,000 a year** (middle half $41,600 to $97,500).
2. **53% of postings quote an hourly rate** and 44% an annual salary; hourly postings annualise (× 2,080 hours) to a median $43,680, against $88,000 for annual-salary postings.
3. **DevOps & cloud has the highest median** ($126,950), then software engineering ($120,805) and product & project management ($115,000); retail & hospitality is lowest ($36,816).
4. **Highest-paying states** (1,000+ postings): District of Columbia ($85,000), California ($70,000) and New York ($68,640); lowest: Oklahoma ($45,760). California holds 22% of postings.
5. **San Francisco–Oakland–Berkeley is the best-paying large metro** (median $98,500), ahead of San Jose–Sunnyvale–Santa Clara ($96,550); Jacksonville is lowest among metros with 1,000+ postings ($49,000).
6. **Seniority ladder**: entry $41,600, mid $70,000, senior $100,000, manager $83,200, director $130,000; remote-marked postings pay a median $88,000 against $59,700 onsite.
us-salary-benchmarks-2026.method:
1. **Scope.** Postings located in the United States with a title, an employer and stated pay, published 2024-01-01 to 2026-06-30.
2. **Deduplication.** Postings with the same employer, normalised title and month are one posting; the copy with the most structured fields is kept.
3. **Annualisation.** Hourly × 2,080, daily × 260, weekly × 52, bi-weekly × 26, semi-monthly × 24, monthly × 12. Postings without a currency are taken as US$. A lower bound below a tenth of the upper bound is treated as missing, and the midpoint is then the single figure.
4. **Absurd values dropped.** Annual pay below US$15,000 or above US$1,000,000; weekly travel-contract healthcare pay that was annualised as if it were a yearly figure; hourly rates above US$150 or weekly above US$5,000 outside professional roles (per-load or per-mile figures); more than US$200,000 for low-wage titles such as cook, cashier or driver; and a non-US currency (411 postings in all: weekly travel-contract pay mislabelled 297, implausible for role 59, currency differs from country 37, implausible hourly rate 10, below floor 7, implausible weekly rate 1).
5. **Labels.** `role_family` from the posting, else keyword rules on the title, else the category. `seniority` from the posting or title, else from years asked (≤1 entry, 2–5 mid, 6–10 senior, 11+ lead). `metro` groups principal cities of each metro area. `remote` from the posting's work-mode field and "remote" / "hybrid" in the title.
6. **Privacy and provenance.** URLs, source names, descriptions and recruiter details are not published; posting IDs are hashes. Postings whose employer or title names a job board or data provider are dropped.
7. **Company link.** `company_domain` is filled only when the lower-cased employer name matches exactly one US company in Fliar's index.

8. **Sample.** Each company key is ranked by `sha1(key)`. Keys are taken in rank order until the file holds max(25%, 5,000) rows (capped at 100,000).

9. **Profile links.** Links are built from Fliar's company index and checked against it. A row whose company has no public profile has an empty link.
us-salary-benchmarks-2026.limitations:
- Pay-transparency laws make postings from some states (California, Colorado, Washington, New York) far more likely to state pay, so those states are over-represented.
- Posted pay is an offer range, not realised pay; it usually excludes bonus, equity and benefits.
- Collection grows sharply in 2026 (April–June 2026 hold most rows), so month-to-month changes mix collection with hiring.
- Hourly pay is annualised at 2,080 hours; part-time and per-diem roles are therefore overstated as annual income.
- Staffing agencies post on behalf of clients and appear as the employer.
- Role families and seniority are keyword-based and can be wrong for unusual titles; seniority is blank for many postings.

8. **Location check.** Companies whose rounds mostly name cities that are almost never in the United States across the global table (under 5% of 10 or more rounds) are dropped: their website was matched to a same-named foreign company, or the company only has a holding entity here.
9. **Back-fill days.** Two days on which archives of older articles were loaded with the load date instead of the publication date (2024-04-22 and 2025-02-13) are excluded.
10. **State.** From the company's record in the company register; when it has none, the most common state of companies in the same city in this data.

11. **Sample.** Each company key is ranked by `sha1(key)`. Keys are taken in rank order until the file holds max(25%, 5,000) rows (capped at 100,000).

12. **Profile links.** Links are built from Fliar's company index and checked against it. A row whose company has no public profile has an empty link.

vc-investor-directory.title: VC Investor Directory 2026: 35k Startup Investors
vc-investor-directory.description: VC investor directory of 35,310 startup investors (VC, CVC, PE, accelerators) ranked by funding rounds worldwide, 2019 to mid-2026, with sector and stage mix.
vc-investor-directory.acquisition:
**How this dataset was acquired.** Every row is aggregated from the [Radar API](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp), Fliar's company-data API and MCP server.
Radar reads business news continuously and extracts each startup funding announcement into structured fields: company, stage,
amount, date and every named investor. Those rounds are cleaned (repeated reports merged, recaps dropped, amounts checked against
the source sentence) and the investors are then aggregated here: one row per investor organisation, with its deal count, lead
count, stage mix, sectors and countries from January 2019 to June 2026. Individual angels and any name that reads as a person are
removed. The investor profile with the full portfolio is available through `POST /v1/investors/page`
([reference](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp/blob/main/docs/reference/get_investor_page.md)) or the `get_investor_page` MCP tool; `POST /v1/investors/search` finds investors by filters.
vc-investor-directory.sample_note:
**This file is a 25% sample: 8,827 of 35,310 investors.** It keeps every record for a fixed subset of investors.
The subset is chosen by a hash, so it stays the same from one release to the next. The findings and tables below were computed
on the **full** data. For the rest, the withheld fields and monthly updates, [get a Radar API key](https://fliarbi.com/radar-api/developer) ([docs](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp)).
Each row's `fliar_profile_url` opens the company's full profile on Fliar.
vc-investor-directory.findings:
1. **35,310 investor organisations joined 64,799 funding rounds between January 2019 and June 2026.** 16,168 of them (46%) appear in two or more rounds; 3,988 appear in ten or more.
2. **The ten most active investors joined 6,051 rounds** (9% of all rounds with a named organisation investor). Y Combinator leads with 1,090 rounds, followed by Tiger Global (897) and Accel (865).
3. **Venture firms are 69% of investors**, but the round sizes they join differ by type: the median round joined by a typical PE investor is $93.6M, against $8.6M for VC firms and $2.7M for accelerators.
4. **12,702 investors were active in 2022, the peak year.** In 2025, 9,038 were active and 2,577 made their first round in the data.
5. **Leading is concentrated.** Only 300 investors led 10 or more rounds. The most frequent leads were Y Combinator (116), Softbank (101), BGF (100).
6. **Where investors are based** (for the 16,930 with a known headquarters): United States 6,641, United Kingdom 1,270, India 1,228, China 596, Canada 563.
vc-investor-directory.method:
1. **Source rounds.** The cleaned global startup funding table (January 2019 to June 2026, companies founded in 2000 or later, venture-style instruments only, repeated reports merged within 45 days). Two days on which archives of older articles were loaded with the load date instead of the publication date (2024-04-22 and 2025-02-13, about 1,200 rounds) are excluded.
2. **Organisations only.** An investor name is kept when it reads as an organisation and not as a person: generic phrases ("angel investors", "undisclosed", "existing investors"), names with a personal title (founder, CEO, partner at ...), "First Last" names whose first word is a given name learned from the data, and possessive or descriptive phrases are dropped. Names of data providers are dropped.
3. **Aliases.** Spellings are merged on a key that ignores case, punctuation and suffixes such as Capital, Ventures, Partners, LLC and Ltd, plus a short list of known aliases (a16z = Andreessen Horowitz, Peak XV = Sequoia Capital India). Distinct regional arms such as "Matrix Partners India" stay separate.
4. **Lead.** A round counts as led when any report of it flagged the investor as lead, or when it was the only investor named. Many reports name no lead, so lead counts are lower bounds.
5. **Website and headquarters.** The website is the news-reported domain whose name matches the investor; it is rejected when the company register lists that domain as an unrelated business. Six of the most active investors have a hand-checked website. Headquarters country and city come from the company record behind that website, or from a country in the name.
6. **Type, by rule (first match wins).** accelerator (accelerator, incubator, studio names); government (public agencies, development banks, sovereign funds); CVC (venture arms of corporates and banks, and corporates investing directly); bank-debt (banks, lenders and investors whose rounds are mostly debt); PE (buyout, growth-equity and asset-management names, or 60%+ growth rounds with a median round of US$50M+); VC (venture names, investment-firm records or mostly staged venture rounds); other (angel networks, family offices, foundations, pension and insurance money, crowdfunding platforms, the rest).
7. **Stage mix.** Seed = pre-seed, angel, seed; early = pre-Series A to Series B; growth = Series C and later plus growth/PE. Shares use staged rounds only. `median_round_usd` is the median disclosed size of the whole rounds it joined, not its own cheque.

8. **Sample.** Each investor key is ranked by `sha1(key)`. Keys are taken in rank order until the file holds max(25%, 5,000) rows (capped at 100,000).

9. **Profile links.** Links are built from Fliar's company index and checked against it. A row whose company has no public profile has an empty link.
vc-investor-directory.limitations:
- Built from news: rounds that were never reported are missing, and coverage is stronger for larger and English-reported deals.
- Investor names come from article text, so a small number of aliases stay split and a few unrelated firms with the same normalised name may be merged.
- Lead investors are often not reported; `lead_deals` is a lower bound.
- Websites are matched for fewer than half of the investors, and headquarters for a similar share; a matched website can occasionally belong to a same-named company.
- Types are rule-based and approximate, especially the boundary between VC, PE and asset managers.
- 2026 covers January to June only.

vc-pe-fund-raises.title: VC & PE Fund Raises 2010–2026
vc-pe-fund-raises.description: Venture, private equity, infrastructure, real estate and credit fund raises with size and manager
vc-pe-fund-raises.acquisition:
**How this dataset was acquired.** Every row comes from the [Radar API](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp), Fliar's company-data API and MCP server. Radar reads
business news continuously and extracts each announcement of a new investment fund into structured fields: the manager, the fund name and
type, the target and amount raised, the close date, the sector and geographic focus and any anchor investors. It then links the manager to
its record in a database of five million companies. This release covers venture capital, private equity, infrastructure, real estate and
private credit funds reported from January 2010 to June 2026. Repeat reports of the same fund are merged, and every amount is checked
against the sentence it was read from. Each row names the article it was read from (`news_source`, `news_url`) and quotes the sentence
(`news_excerpt`). A manager's full, continuously updated event timeline, including fund raises, is available through
`POST /v1/companies/events` ([reference](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp/blob/main/docs/reference/get_company_events.md)) or the `get_company_events` MCP tool.
vc-pe-fund-raises.sample_note:
**This file is a 25% sample: 5,591 of 22,361 fund raises.** It keeps every record for a fixed subset of managers.
The subset is chosen by a hash, so it stays the same from one release to the next. The findings and tables below were computed
on the **full** data. For the rest, the withheld fields and monthly updates, [get a Radar API key](https://fliarbi.com/radar-api/developer) ([docs](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp)).
Each row's `fliar_profile_url` opens the company's full profile on Fliar.
vc-pe-fund-raises.findings:
1. **22,361 fund raises by 9,965 managers, 2010 to June 2026.** 14,695 disclosed a raised amount, totalling $9.3T.
2. **2022 was the busiest year** with 2,382 fund raises reported; 2025 had 1,932 ($723.6B disclosed).
3. **Venture capital is the most common fund type** (12,578 funds), but private equity raised the most disclosed money ($5.1T vs $2.0T).
4. **Billion-dollar funds hold the money:** 1,865 funds of US$1B or more are 13% of funds with an amount but 75% of disclosed dollars.
5. **Targets vs closes:** of 8,751 funds reporting both, the median raised 100% of target and 77% met or beat it.
6. **Geography:** the top three countries by disclosed fund size (United States, United Kingdom, India) account for 66% of disclosed dollars with a country.
vc-pe-fund-raises.method:
1. **Extraction.** Radar's pipeline reads each article about a new fund and extracts structured fields, including the source sentence.
2. **Scope.** Venture capital, private equity, infrastructure (including energy), real estate, private credit and fund-of-funds vehicles. Mutual funds, hedge funds and ETFs are dropped, as are rows with no fund type unless the name says "fund", and rows that describe a company's own funding round.
3. **Manager.** The manager name comes from Fliar's company database when its website is known. Names that read as individuals are blanked, and social-profile links are removed from the domain field.
4. **Deduplication.** Reports are merged per manager (name variants such as "Blackstone Group" and "The Blackstone Group" count as one). The same numbered fund name (roman and ordinal numbers normalised, "Fund IX" = "Ninth Fund") is one fund at any distance in time. Otherwise, within 540 days of a fund's first report, reports merge when the fund name matches, when the amount matches within 3%, or when one report is unnamed and close in time (45 days). A US$1B+ amount re-reported by the same manager or under the same fund name (within 1%, 540 days) is the same fund. Otherwise funds with different numbers never merge. The largest checked close is kept.
5. **Amount check.** Each amount is compared with the money figures parsed from its source sentence (tolerance 0.6–1.7×), allowing for amounts stored in millions. `verified` matched; `unchecked` had no parseable figure; `failed_check` is blank because it did not match, was a bare number under 10,000, was over US$5B without a match, or was over US$20B (US$30B) without two (three) or more reports and a known manager website; `not_disclosed` had no amount.
6. **Currency.** US dollars, from the stored conversion or at fixed approximate rates.
7. **Bulk back-fills.** Days carrying more than five times the usual number of reports (archive back-fills stamped with an ingest date rather than the publication date) are dropped.
8. **Dates.** The date is the earliest report's publication date; rows before 2010 or after June 2026 are dropped.

9. **Sample.** Each manager key is ranked by `sha1(key)`. Keys are taken in rank order until the file holds max(25%, 5,000) rows (capped at 100,000).

10. **Profile links.** Links are built from Fliar's company index and checked against it. A row whose company has no public profile has an empty link.
vc-pe-fund-raises.limitations:
- Derived from news: funds that were never reported are missing, and coverage favours large, English-reported funds.
- The date is the article date. An article can describe a fund closed earlier.
- A raised amount can be an interim close rather than the final size.
- Fund types and focus are as reported and classified; the focus grouping is keyword-based.
- Individuals named as managers are blanked, so some rows have no manager.
- `news_source` and `news_url` are blank when the article could not be retrieved at release time.

website-technology-stack.title: Website Technology Stack of 2M Companies (2026)
website-technology-stack.description: Technologies, CMS, CDN and page speed detected on 2M company websites
website-technology-stack.acquisition:
**How this dataset was acquired.** Every row comes from the [Radar API](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp), Fliar's company-data API and MCP server. Radar keeps
a database of five million companies and runs its own website crawls over their domains (Fliar website crawls). Each crawl loads the
home page and records the technologies and site features it can detect from the page code, headers and network calls: content
management systems, JavaScript frameworks, analytics and ad tags, payment and e-mail services, hosting and CDN. It also grades page
speed and on-page SEO. This release keeps one row per company domain for the 2 million companies whose site returned a detectable stack,
with the company's country and sector from Radar's company records. The full data is available through `POST /v1/companies/field` with
`"field": "technology"` ([reference](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp/blob/main/docs/reference/get_company_field.md)) or the `get_company_field` MCP tool.
website-technology-stack.sample_note:
**This file is a 5% sample: 100,000 of 2,079,163 company websites.** It keeps every record for a fixed subset of domains.
The subset is chosen by a hash, so it stays the same from one release to the next. The findings and tables below were computed
on the **full** data. For the rest, the withheld fields and monthly updates, [get a Radar API key](https://fliarbi.com/radar-api/developer) ([docs](https://github.com/fliarbi/radar-api-mcp)).
Each row's `fliar_profile_url` opens the company's full profile on Fliar.
website-technology-stack.findings:
1. **2,079,163 company websites, 3,538 distinct technologies.** The median site runs 17 detected technologies; 16% run 30 or more.
2. **jQuery is still everywhere.** It is on 72% of sites, ahead of PHP (60%) and Google Analytics (56%).
3. **WordPress runs 47% of company websites**; Shopify runs 4.4%, Wix 3.6% and Squarespace 3.0%. 35% of sites show none of the 18 site platforms tracked here.
4. **Popular sites use modern front-ends more.** React is on 34% of sites ranked in the global top 1M, against 14% of all sites.
5. **Cloudflare dominates delivery.** Cloudflare code or headers show up on 44% of sites. 30% of sites have an identified serving CDN, and Cloudflare is that CDN for 64% of them.
6. **Google's tags are near-universal in marketing stacks.** Google Tag Manager is on 35% of sites and the Facebook pixel on 19%.
website-technology-stack.method:
1. **Detection.** Technologies are matched from page HTML, scripts, headers, cookies and DNS of the company's home page. A technology missing from the list may still be in use on other pages or server-side.
2. **One row per domain.** Domains are lowercased with `www.` removed. When one domain appears under several company records, the crawl with the most detected technologies is kept.
3. **Country and sector.** Country names are normalised (for example "england, united kingdom", "uk" and "united kingdom (uk)" become "United Kingdom"); values that are not a country are blank. The sector is the first practice area from Radar's company classifier.
4. **Removed.** A handful of tracking tags named after data providers are removed from the technology lists, as are companies whose name or domain names a data provider. No e-mail addresses or phone numbers are published.
5. **Shares.** Every share in the tables is computed on the full table of company websites, not on the sample.

6. **Sample.** Each domain key is ranked by `sha1(key)`. Keys are taken in rank order until the file holds max(25%, 5,000) rows (capped at 100,000).

7. **Profile links.** Links are built from Fliar's company index and checked against it. A row whose company has no public profile has an empty link.
website-technology-stack.limitations:
- Detection sees the public home page only: back-end systems, intranets and apps behind a login are invisible.
- Coverage is of companies in Radar's database, so it leans toward companies with an online presence and toward English-speaking markets.
- Country is unknown for a share of sites and sector for a smaller share; they are blank, not guessed.
- Crawls were made at different dates (mostly 2026); a site may have changed its stack since.
- Page-speed and SEO grades are blank when the crawl could not measure them.
